Acknowledgments: Special thanks to Eric Stride and Andrea Hatcher for their contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Background

On October 16, Huntress first reported the abuse of a ConnectWise Cloud Backup credential to access Microsoft 365 tenants, and since then we have been continuing to investigate threat actor behavior related to this incident.

Now, we're pulling on a different thread: who, or what, was doing the typing during the unauthorized activity we observed. Microsoft has published its own findings, attributing the activity to a threat actor it tracks as Storm-0940, which it says used ARTEX, an open-source multi-agent AI framework, to abuse the compromised ConnectWise application credentials and sign in to downstream Microsoft 365 tenants at machine speed. Our telemetry aligns with Microsoft's findings, but does not independently confirm them.

In the activity on the tenants we examined, we observed the tooling change in under a minute between runs and a retry loop appear in the run after a failure. Some actions were tested in one tenant before being run in batches, a pattern we saw three times across two tools.

Taken together, these observations form our working hypothesis: scripted tooling did most of the heavy lifting in this incident, while something adapted the tooling between runs, quickly. That something may very well be an agent. Below, we're providing details about what we saw, and leaving it to the audience to draw their own conclusions.

What we can and cannot see

Our view comes from Entra Sign-in logs and directory audit logs in the Microsoft 365 tenants we monitor, plus the fleet-wide sweeps we ran during the incident window. That gives us the timing, order, and shape of what the actor caused Entra to record. However, it leaves some large gaps:

Microsoft Graph reads are not recorded in the Entra audit log, and no victim we know of had Graph activity logging enabled, so the scope and method of any Graph access cannot be seen in the logs available to us.

Application-only audit events carry no source IP address, so we cannot tie some of the activity, such as the credential changes, to a specific IP.

We have no visibility into the actor's own systems, so we cannot see the tooling itself, or whether any model provider sat behind it.

Lastly, we cannot say whether AI was used to plan the operation, develop target lists, or write the tooling.

One day, three modes of operation

Most of what we can see happened on October 15, in a little under 14 hours. Laid out in a single timeline, the activity falls into three distinct behaviors:

Scripted loops

Hands-on operator work (an "operator" being whoever steered the tooling, whether that's a person, automation, or an AI agent)

A stretch where the tooling kept running after the thing it was targeting was already gone

Figure 1: Activity on October 15 in Huntress-monitored tenants, grouped by behavior. Operator-driven means a person, or a model acting for one, was steering the tooling between runs.

How scripts, people, and AI agents look different in logs

The logs Huntress analyzes record behavior and help us figure out what occurred: how fast things happen, what happens after something fails, and how much the requests vary. The logs may show different types of fingerprints depending on if the behavior comes from a script, a person, or an LLM agent. Below is a table of possible behavioral signals between the three, though these are general characteristics and may have substantial overlap.

Signal

Scripted automation

Human operator

LLM agent in the loop

Pacing

Machine-regular, sub-second or fixed intervals

Uneven, with pauses that look like reading output

Steady, gated by model inference

Response to errors

None unless coded, repeats the same failure

Reads the error, adjusts, or gives up

Reads the error and changes approach

Variety of requests

Identical request shape, repeated

Efficient, goes to what it wants

Exploratory, retries with variations

User agent

One fixed string per tool

Varies with the tools the person picks up

Often SDK defaults (python-requests, httpx)

These categories are Huntress analyst heuristics for telling the three apart, not an industry standard. A tricky nuance here is that this isn't a black-or-white determination: no single row completely settles what's primarily behind the attack. For instance, a script can carry a sleep timer and a list of user agents, which could make its behaviors in the logs look more human than it is. One password spray against a single tenant may at first read like a person, but a fixed beat in the timing and a rotating list of user agents would indicate otherwise. When investigating these signals, part of what matters is the mix and whether the behavior changes in response to what just happened. A script repeats itself; a person or an agent adjusts.

Two limits apply to everything in our analysis below:

A person pasting commands from a chatbot into a terminal looks like a person in these logs, because the model never touches the API.

Logs show who ran the tooling, not who wrote it; a model can write a fixed script that looks like any other script.

What we saw

The loops: scripts at scale

The logs showed us that on October 15, between roughly 06:13 and 08:46 UTC, the credential was used against almost 1,000 tenants, one after another, in ascending tenant ID order. That is a loop over a sorted list: one token request per tenant, one to six minutes apart, with the same user agent (Python-urllib/3.12) every time. When the loop stopped partway through the list, it looked like an exhausted list or an interrupted process (as opposed to a concerted decision to stop).

The logs also showed that nine minutes earlier, around 06:04 UTC, about 100 failed token requests had landed within 10 seconds against the first 100 tenants of that same list of 1,000 tenants. Every request failed the same way, and nothing changed between attempts. This is a signature of a thread pool: a fixed set of worker threads pulling tenants off a shared list and firing requests in parallel, each blind to what the others get back. Nothing in the loop reads a response before the next request goes out.

The same thread-pool tool then ran a second time against 100 tenants, using a different application's key, at 13 to 21 attempts per second, and failed the same way. Both runs used application secrets that belong to a single tenant, which cannot authenticate anywhere else, and the tool kept firing regardless. Whoever built it, or at least launched it, did not account for that difference.

Here is what that does and does not tell us: 10 requests a second is faster than anything that reads each response before deciding its next move, whether that is a person or a model working step by step. So this was most likely one script, run at least twice. It does not tell us who or what wrote the script. A model can write a thread pool as easily as a person can, so while this rules out a model making each call, it does not rule out a model writing the tool.

Trial and error

On October 15 between 03:42 and 03:57 UTC, the logs indicated a pattern of trial and error in the unauthorized activity, with the tooling changing in less than a minute between runs. The activity outlined in the logs looked like an attempt to establish persistent access by adding credentials:

A secret was added, removed, and added again.

A certificate was uploaded, but it failed because the thumbprint did not match.

The operator fell back to a secret again before granting, then removing, the Global Administrator role twice.

The same sequence ran in a second tenant 47 seconds later, with both keys added in a single run.

During that window the tooling changed in response to results at least three times. The run after the failed certificate upload added a retry loop, the sequence repeated in a second tenant with both keys in a single run, and when that tenant refused a Global Administrator removal, the actor granted a different role to a sibling principal, and the original service principal was then deleted.

Based on this activity, it's possible that the credential planting and the targeted probe were steered by an operator adapting between runs. However, we can't determine whether that operator was a person, automation, or an LLM model.

The hand-picked targets: pilot, then batch

Between roughly 09:25 and 12:35 UTC on October 15, one sweep touched 17 tenants, with one Graph token request each in a hand-ordered sequence with irregular spacing over three hours. A second sweep at 13:54 UTC ran a fixed probe of six resources per tenant, in sorted order, with four seconds per tenant. Someone appears to have chosen the targets, checked them one at a time, and then handed the list to a script.

Where it started to look like an agent

No single observation here proves anything, and we are not going to pretend otherwise. But several of them pointed in the same direction, and the longer we looked, the harder it became to explain them away as a person at a keyboard or a script left to run.

First, there's the 55-second gap between retries that we described above. The certificate upload that failed on a thumbprint mismatch at 03:48:24 UTC ended that run with no retry. The next run, 55 seconds later, did retry the same error, at 3.5 seconds and then 7.1 seconds, until it worked, and it carried the same retry into the second tenant.

Figure 2: How the tooling changed

So what does this actually tell us about what was going on behind the scenes? Either someone edited the code in under a minute, or a prepared tool had a retry option nobody had used yet. A script left alone does not rewrite itself between runs. A person, a person relaying to a model, or an agent was likely adapting it as an operator. The speed of the change is consistent with an agent loop: read the failure, rewrite the call, run it again.

The retry logic is particularly revealing. Doubling the wait between attempts is textbook defensive error handling. This is something that generated code tends to add unprompted, and in this incident showed up in a tool that had none just a minute earlier. The tooling was also more elaborate than the job required: the 100-tenant burst used a thread pool, where a simple loop over the list would have done the same work.

Another notable pattern that we outlined above: An operator tried an action against one tenant first, then ran it as a batch, again and again. We saw that three times across two sets of tooling. That points to the habits of an operator, not a quirk of one script. Microsoft describes ARTEX as building a graph of the assets it discovers and running parallel breach paths, which has the same shape: probe, learn, and then fan out.

Finally, there is the speed. Our first enumeration activity started around 01:05 UTC, and the credential changes in the first tenant were complete by 03:50 UTC, in line with Microsoft's report of under three hours from targeting to privileged access in multiple environments. Speed alone does not separate an agent from a well-prepared script, but it is the kind of compression Microsoft describes agent frameworks delivering. Some of the user agent strings also look hand-set rather than library defaults. One tool identified itself as python-requests/2.31, where the library sends python-requests/2.31.0 by default, and on October 13 a browser string was missing its standard "(KHTML, like Gecko)" segment. Both fit a model producing user agents from memory, and both fit a person copying them from documentation.

Put together, these factors make up our working hypothesis: scripted tooling is doing the heavy lifting in this incident, with something adapting it between runs, quickly. That something may well be an agent. The next section is about how sure we are, and where the evidence runs out.

What the telemetry can confirm

A working hypothesis is only worth sharing if its limits are clear. Here are ours.

The best evidence against a fully autonomous agent is what happened after 03:57 UTC. The Teams service principal was deleted, and for the next 22 minutes requests using it kept firing every four to eight seconds. These were rejected every time, and subsequent requests didn't change. An agent watching its own output would be expected to stop. A multi-agent framework could keep unattended fan-out tasks running while other agents carry on, which could explain this behavior. So too could a person who launched some background loops and walked away. However we don't know which one played out in this situation.

Another consideration: curl/7.88.1 is the version Debian 12 ships with, and the official python:3.12 container image is built on Debian 12. That points to how the tooling was possibly packaged, since the user agent doesn't align with the system's external fingerprints.

The biggest gap is the missing Graph request logs. They would show query variety, the clearest difference between a script and an agent, and nobody we know of collected them.

So, how sure are we? We are highly confident that an operator, whether a person or an LLM model, adapted the tooling between runs. On our own telemetry alone, we put our confidence that an LLM was involved in the escalation tooling at low to medium. Taking Microsoft's attribution into account, we put it at medium to high.

What would potentially help settle it is evidence we do not hold: the Graph activity logs from a victim that had them enabled, the tooling itself, or traffic from the actor's systems to a model provider's API.

What Microsoft says: Storm-0940 and ARTEX

In its October 21 report Microsoft attributes the ConnectWise credential abuse to Storm-0940, a threat actor they say has been active since 2021. Microsoft asserts that the actor targets organizations across industries for data theft, and has historically gotten in through password spraying and internet-facing applications, then kept access by adding credentials to existing OAuth applications.

What is new, according to Microsoft, is the tooling. They report that from at least September 2026 the actor used ARTEX, an open-source framework in which LLM-driven agents run a penetration test from reconnaissance through data exfiltration with little needed human interaction, building a graph of the assets and weaknesses they discover as they go. ARTEX can use any AI model, and Microsoft says it has seen other actors using it in several regions.

How does Microsoft connect that to this incident? The reasoning they've shared points to infrastructure, attributing a large password spray from 144.172.64[.]99 between October 10 and 14 to Storm-0940, and noting that the same IP, and the surrounding range, appear in the ConnectWise advisory. The report does not describe how Microsoft identified ARTEX, or what links the earlier spray to Storm-0940. We have not independently verified either. However, Microsoft may know how to identify this particular tooling, which is why they have mentioned its usage in this campaign.

How our findings line up with Microsoft's report

Our telemetry is consistent with Microsoft's account in several ways.

We saw the same infrastructure (144.172.64[.]128) and user agents (Python-urllib/3.12, curl/7.88.1), and the same sequence: compromised application credentials, then Graph follow-on with credential additions and privileged role changes, including the Teams application assigning itself Global Administrator.

Our telemetry also corroborates the password spray Microsoft attributes to 144.172.64[.]99.

Scale is where we differ, by design. Microsoft counts more than 2,250 tenants and we see only the tenants we protect, so our numbers are only a subset, not a contradiction. We saw python-requests/2.34.2 from 144.172.64[.]99 in the October 10 to 14 password spray, but not azure-toolkit/1.0, and we saw no identity or group changes in the two tenants where we hold directory audit logs.

Why this matters

Whoever, or whatever was behind it, this operation was not polished. Over the course of our investigation we saw:

Secrets added, removed, and added again.

A certificate that failed to upload.

Secrets for one tenant sprayed at a hundred others, where they would never work.

Yet, as we saw in the two tenants where we hold audit logs, it took under three hours from the first enumeration activity to privileged role changes, in line with Microsoft's report across multiple environments, because the stolen application credential did much of the work.

It's clumsy, but it worked. If an agent was in the loop here, it was an early one. It already ran things in parallel, never needed a break, and left defenders a few hours. Tools like this get better quickly: they stop making the mistakes we saw, and they are cheap to point at hundreds of tenants at once. Microsoft makes the same point: agents can work around the clock and attempt multiple breach paths simultaneously.

Defenders' visibility is also in flux. In our view, the signals we relied on here (a retry that showed up 55 seconds after a failure, a fixed beat between requests, and user agent strings customized away from the library default) are the first things a better tool will smooth away. Cadence will not be a reliable signal for long. What will hold up is what the activity does, which is where the detections below point.

What defenders can do

Speed is the biggest concern here. This activity moves faster than a person can triage. This is useful detection guidance regardless of the actor:

Alert when a service principal assigns itself Global Administrator or Privileged Role Administrator, deletes itself, or when one vendor principal grants a role to a sibling.

Alert on credential additions to high-privilege applications from unexpected sources.

Baseline each vendor application's normal user agent (kiota-dotnet for the ConnectWise applications), source ranges, and cadence. The clearest early signal here was a vendor application behaving differently from its baseline.

Turn on Microsoft Graph activity logs where licensing allows, and keep raw user agent strings and sub-second timestamps. Cadence and retry timing were our most useful signals, and normalization destroys both.

Watch across tenants, not only within one. A trickle in any single tenant can be one campaign running at thousands of attempts per minute across the estate.

We will update this post as ConnectWise, Microsoft, and others share more.

Title: M365 Token Spray and Replay Campaign Compromises Business Email Accounts
Context: Microsoft independently flagged the same infrastructure: Microsoft Entra ID Protection raised verified threat actor IP detections against 193
Full Text:
Acknowledgments: Special thanks to Anton Ovrutsky for his contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Background

Between July 14, 2026 and September 22, 2026, Huntress detected 497 Microsoft 365 sign-in events across 79 victim organizations related to a token replay campaign using an IP address block from the German hosting provider 1337 Services GmbH. Rather than guessing passwords, the attacker replayed sign-in tokens stolen from victims, and we've traced more than 200,000 failed login attempts from the campaign window back to the 193.26.115[.]0/24 IP range.

Figure 1: Overall statistics of the activity Huntress observed

Figure 2: Successful sign-in events using token replays over the course of the campaign

Also known as AS210558, 1337 Services GmbH is incorporated in Hamburg, Germany. While 1337 Services GmbH offers a legitimate IP hosting service, attackers use these kinds of ISP providers to host malicious traffic, a tactic referred to as "bring your own IP" (BYOIP). A February 2025 Krebs on Security article suggests that 1337 Services GmbH's founder may have operated the Cracked cybercrime forum.

The Microsoft accounts were compromised without the attacker ever needing a password. In an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) attack, the victim signs in through a relay that sits between them and Microsoft. The relay passes the real login page and MFA prompt through to the victim, then keeps the "proof of login" token Microsoft issues once the victim finishes signing in. Because that token is minted after MFA, whoever holds it doesn't need to pass MFA again. The threat actor then replayed the stolen tokens from their own machines in automated sign-in attempts against Microsoft 365 services. Because the attacker replayed many stolen tokens at volume across many organizations, we refer to this as "token spraying:" the same pattern as password spraying, but with stolen tokens instead of guessed passwords.

In this campaign, tokens came from multiple sources: AiTM relays behind fake sign-in pages, device-code phishing, and social engineering during a legitimate login process.

Huntress first detected this activity on July 14, 2026, when a sign-in from 193.26.115[.]221 came from an Entra-joined device named DESKTOP- plus eight hex characters. Microsoft independently flagged the same infrastructure: Microsoft Entra ID Protection raised verified threat actor IP detections against 193.26.115[.]221, 193.26.115[.]72, 193.26.115[.]16, and 193.26.115[.]21 in multiple customer tenants. Microsoft describes this detection as "sign-in activity that is consistent with known IP addresses associated with nation state actors or cyber crime groups, based on Microsoft Security Intelligence (MSTIC)."

A July 21 detection from 193.26.115[.]199 gave us a view of how the attacker was able to steal and reuse a token in less than an hour:

Time (UTC)

Event

17:18:20

An AiTM relay at 185.238.2[.]195 caught the victim at the MFA prompt

17:30:21

The session was hijacked from 193.26.115[.]199

17:43:15

The same session was in use from a second 1337 Services address, 124.198.132[.]33

18:08:50

A new authenticator app, labeled "iPhone 13", was activated on the account

Registering their own authenticator app is a persistence method. A stolen session token eventually expires or gets revoked, but an MFA method stays on the account. With their own authenticator registered, the attacker can complete MFA for new sign-ins whenever they want, and that access survives a password reset unless someone audits the account's MFA methods and removes the rogue one. In 19 organizations, the victim's existing MFA methods were wiped and a new method registered within three hours of the first sign-in from a campaign address.

Rogue devices served the same purpose. Across the compromises we investigated, the threat actor registered at least 48 fake computers in victim organizations' Microsoft directories. A registered device can give the attacker a more durable way to request tokens than the stolen session alone, and it stays in the directory until someone deletes it.

We also observed the threat actor setting up hidden email rules in victim inboxes that quietly moved messages from specific contacts out of sight. In at least one case, the threat actor used the email account to send a payroll-related email to an outside contact. None of the email rules were created from the 1337 Services GmbH network; each one came from a different rented or VPN address.

Technical Details

Over the 10-week campaign, the threat actor replayed stolen Microsoft 365 sessions using rented hosts in one block of IP addresses, 193.26.115[.]0/24. They used six addresses in the /24 range, one after another:

Figure 3: IP addresses used throughout the token spraying campaign

We can't state with certainty why the operator rotated addresses, but the effect is clear. A block, alert, or Conditional Access rule written for one address does nothing against the next, and Microsoft flagged addresses individually: its incidents named 193.26.115[.]221, 193.26.115[.]72, 193.26.115[.]16, and 193.26.115[.]21, not the range. Several switches followed a quiet period, about two weeks between Phases 1 and 2 and a week before the September 22 takeover. Blocking any single address would have stopped one phase at most. Blocking the /24 would have covered all six main replay hosts, though the operator also used a few other 1337 Services addresses outside it.

Two tiers: relays capture, 1337 replays

The operator split the attack across two kinds of infrastructure. First, the victim signs in through an AiTM relay. The relay passes the victim's MFA prompt through and keeps the resulting session. Then, within minutes, the stolen session reappears from a 1337 Services address. On July 21, the gap between the victim reaching the MFA prompt and the hijacked session appearing was 12 minutes. On September 22, it was four.

Because the two halves sit on different providers, blocking the 1337 range doesn't stop credentials from being captured, and blocking a relay doesn't stop replay of tokens that were already stolen.

Two builds

The replay hosts ran two distinct toolsets, which we refer to as Build A and Build B:

Attribute

Build A: Scripted token replay

Build B: Browser session replay

Across Build A sign-ins, we observed 48 distinct Entra-joined devices named DESKTOP- plus exactly eight uppercase hexadecimal characters (for example, DESKTOP-54521F46). That doesn't match Windows' own out-of-box default, which is DESKTOP- plus seven alphanumeric characters.

With these shifts in the IP addresses came variations in tradecraft. We tracked four distinct phases throughout the campaign.

Figure 4: Token replay campaign timeline

Phase 1: The July Wave (193.26.115[.]221 and 193.26.115[.]199)

Huntress began observing stolen tokens being used to access more than a dozen organizations starting on July 14, 2026. In 13 of the 14 incidents Huntress responded to on that day, the attacker had registered a fake Windows-style computer in the victim organization's directory, named DESKTOP- plus eight hex characters. These sign-ins all used Build A: the node user agent, replaying tokens through the Microsoft Office client. After registering the rogue device from the 1337 Services GmbH address, the attacker would often pivot to an ExpressVPN or CrownCloud address for further activity. Alongside it, 193.26.115[.]199 ran Build B, replaying browser sessions straight from AiTM relays, as in the July 21 timeline above.

The attacker created malicious email rules in a number of the compromised accounts to delete or move messages with certain keywords to an obscure folder, like RSS Feeds. In one compromised mailbox, an email rule named sss was created to mark all incoming mail as read and then delete it. The attacker then used the mailbox to send outbound spam to hundreds of external recipients before Microsoft Entra ID Protection rated the account high risk, and Huntress disabled the rule.

We last detected activity from the 193.26.115[.]221 IP address on August 3. By then, the attacker had successfully signed in to 37 organizations and registered 37 rogue Entra devices.

Phase 2: The August–September Wave (193.26.115[.]16 and 193.26.115[.]21)

After a two-week gap, the threat actor came back using two new IP addresses on August 17. This burst saw more email-hiding rules, and in one case the threat actor registered a lookalike of a business partner's web address.

This wave also added device-code phishing. We recorded sign-ins through the Microsoft Office device-code flow from 193.26.115[.]16, where the victim is tricked into entering a code on Microsoft's legitimate sign-in page and directly hands and attacker a valid refresh and access token, unknowingly authorizing the attacker's session. The same address also signed in to the Device Registration Service, the endpoint used to join new devices to the tenant. 193.26.115[.]21 replayed tokens against SharePoint Online with a bare Mozilla/5.0 user agent.

In this second wave, we started observing the attacker clearing compromised users' MFA settings to allow for first-time device registration with no device tokens or one-time passwords. The pattern was consistent: the victim's MFA methods were wiped through Microsoft's security-info registration service, and a new authenticator was registered minutes later. In one incident, we observed the threat actor using a deviceless authenticator method that was already on the account.

Phase 3: The September 11 Burst (193.26.115[.]72)

On the afternoon of September 11, the threat actor switched to a new address again, this time running an automated program (user agent node) that reused stolen sign-in passes. Within two hours, Huntress sent incident reports to 22 customers. Every sign-in we recorded from this address used the Microsoft Office or Authentication Broker client and OAuth2:Token requests (the action of trading one token for another), most of them targeting Microsoft Graph. Over four days, the address completed 303 successful sign-ins across 29 organizations.

Conditional Access did real work here. The same address logged 1,052 blocked sign-ins as the attempts continued, but all of those blocks came from just four organizations. In the 29 organizations where it got in, nothing stood in the way.

In one incident, the threat actor used the compromised mailbox to send a payroll-related email to an external CPA's email address. The attacker first modified an inbox rule named s to catch any message mentioning payroll, direct deposit, bank, or bonus. Five minutes later, from the same Interserver address (167.148.41[.]96), they created a second rule named d that marked all email from the CPA's address as read and moved it to the Conversation History folder, effectively hiding the responses from the victim.

Phase 4: Relay and replay, September 2–22 (193.26.115[.]210)

The final address paired an AiTM relay at a different hosting provider, Evoxt Sdn. Bhd. (2400:8d60:2::1:841d:5dd), with replay from 193.26.115[.]210. It first appeared on September 2. On September 3, the attacker tried to replay, from 193.26.115[.]210, the session stolen the day before, but the session was no longer valid and the attempt failed with Microsoft's SsoArtifactRevoked error (AADSTS50133).

After a full week of quiet following the Phase 3 burst, we detected one final session takeover on September 22. The victim reached the MFA prompt through the Evoxt relay at 20:46 UTC and completed it a minute later, from a macOS browser using the OfficeHome client. At 20:50, the attacker replayed the session from 193.26.115[.]210. Routing through a Remote Desktop Protocol VDI tunnel operator, the session's OS changed from macOS to Windows, and the threat actor accessed the victim's email.

Post-compromise: Hidden inbox rules

Every suspicious inbox rule we found on accounts compromised in this campaign was created from VPN or rented hosting, never from 1337 Services: ExpressVPN, NordVPN, CrownCloud, DataWagon, GLOBALTELEHOST, LeaseWeb, Dynu, and Interserver. The rule names were deliberately forgettable:

In four mailboxes, rules were created through the Outlook REST API rather than Outlook itself, two of them within minutes of the first sign-in from a campaign address.

The stolen session stopped working

The operator kept coming back. In one organization, they tried to reuse the same stolen session three more times in August: once from 193.26.115[.]199 and twice from other 1337 Services addresses (45.83.31[.]44 and 192.159.99[.]172). Every attempt failed with Microsoft's SsoArtifactRevoked error (AADSTS50133), which Microsoft returns when a session is no longer valid after a password expires or is changed. Although the refresh token and session cookie are expired, the access token will remain valid unless the identity sessions have been revoked or disabled.

Mitigation Guidance: Conditional Access FTW

As we saw in the massive LSHIY password-spraying campaign we reported on earlier this year, Conditional Access Policies (CAP) can help fill some of the security gaps that MFA can't, as long as they're appropriately implemented. Businesses setting up CAPs should require MFA (or block) for All Users, All Cloud Apps, and All Client App types, unconditionally.

Do not trigger response based on spray volume, as it points at the most-sprayed, least-compromised tenants; prioritize by credential validity instead. Phase 3 shows why: All 1,052 of 193.26.115[.]72's blocked sign-ins came from four organizations, and its 232 successful sign-ins landed in 28 different organizations, with no overlap between the two groups. Ranking tenants by failed attempts would have pointed responders at the four where Conditional Access was already working.

If you suspect a token replay compromise:

Revoke sessions and reset the password. A password reset alone does not remove attacker-registered devices or MFA methods. Additionally, you must revoke sessions; a password reset alone does not invalidate the access token, which means the attacker could keep access until the token expires (Time to live of approximately 90 minutes)

Audit Entra devices. Investigate devices named DESKTOP-, Device-, or Work Pc plus eight hex characters, especially ones registered from hosting IP addresses. The pattern is rare, but not unique to this campaign, so confirm before deleting.

Audit MFA methods. Look for MFA methods cleared and then re-registered within minutes, and remove any authenticator the user doesn't recognize.

Review inbox rules. Look for rules with one to three-character or punctuation-only names, rules that move mail to RSS Feeds, RSS Subscriptions, or Conversation History, and rules keyed on payroll or banking terms.

Treat Conditional Access blocks (AADSTS53003) as a sign of a valid credential, not a save. The block happens after authentication succeeds.

Restrict device-code flow with Conditional Access authentication-flow policies. If you need it, create service accounts with restricted permissions and exclusions as necessary.

Hunt for OAuth2:Token and Cmsi:Cmsi sign-ins from hosting infrastructure that use the Microsoft Office or Authentication Broker client with a node or bare Mozilla/5.0 user agent. Expect some legitimate automation; focus on sign-ins that touch user mailboxes or the Device Registration Service.

Hunt for new enterprise applications. Attackers will attempt to maintain persistence by granting new applications access to a tenant, with the level of access varying based on the application's permissions. Better yet, disable the ability for standard users to consent to new applications and instead require users to request new applications.

Title: Amazon-Themed ClickFix Campaign Serves Up Finger-Licking Malware
Context: Introduction Attackers often exploit trusted brands in their initial access lures, either by spoofing their logos or by abusing legitimate features
Full Text:
Introduction

Attackers often exploit trusted brands in their initial access lures, either by spoofing their logos or by abusing legitimate features. In the past few months, Huntress investigated incidents that began with ClickFix lures using ChatGPT, Google Docs, and many more trusted tools. In an attack method that has already struck at least three Huntress customers, a threat actor using paid search results led victims into ClickFix-style social engineering that, as is usually the case, prompts the victims to run a command in their terminal.

But the command used in this lure unusually leverages a decades-old (and infrequently used) network utility, finger, to initiate a convoluted and elaborately obfuscated sequence of attack scripts that, eventually, led to the victim's computer being infected with at least three completely different forms of infostealer and remote access malware. Threat actors have been abusing the finger utility, which (although present on most modern computers) is not well understood by most computer users, in ClickFix attacks for at least a year.

In the course of the investigation, Huntress Labs' Adversary Tactics observed a full infection chain, captured and reverse-engineered the components, and analyzed network traffic sent and received by the various payloads, in order to build a complete picture of the attack method.

A Google search, a spoofed Amazon login, and a fake CAPTCHA

Figure 1: The sponsored Google search result that led to a fake Amazon login page

The attack started with a simple search. The top sponsored result at the time of the attacks for the keyword "amazon business" (shown above) was hosted on a deceptive-looking subdomain of an attacker-controlled domain: orders-amazon[.]com[.]advancedfences[.]com.

The malicious link redirected to a fake Amazon login page, hosted in a private Google Sites cloud storage location, sites.google[.]com/view/ch-pc/sign-in. The page prompted the user to enter their email or phone number.

Figure 2: Spoofed Amazon login page

After the user hits "submit," the page pops up a fake CAPTCHA dialog. Clicking a button labeled "I'm not a robot" saves a pastejacked command to the user's clipboard, and a pop-up window instructs the user to run the command in the Windows Run box.

Figure 3: The ClickFix attack prompts the user to paste a command into their Run dialog on Windows computers

Although the following analysis covers Windows-specific payloads, the attack was cross-platform: Users who visited the page with a browser User-Agent that references macOS received alternate instructions to run a script in the Mac Terminal application, but the destination URL in that instance—hxxp[://]ashevilleroofingcontractor[.]com/curl/bc9e2dac08fb4f83dddb44f89bf7082bb4134697fbf6a99ad8ce30c634e9fe8a—was offline at the time Huntress conducted this research.

Stage 1: Literally giving users the finger

The entered commands launch the built-in utility finger.exe to communicate with a specific user account on the attacker-controlled domain grillrecipespro[.]com.

The finger command is ancient, by internet standards, predating the existence of the web itself by nearly two decades. In its halcyon heyday, people who used the internet would interact directly with Unix shell accounts on remote servers; finger offered a way for someone who owned an account to publish their contact information, a clever quotation or two, even ASCII art to what was essentially a personal bulletin board posted to their virtual office door, inside a file named .plan, stored in the root of the user's shell account directory. But for most of the past year, finger has developed a new life as a LOLbin abused in ClickFix attacks.

In this attack, the threat actor has placed a Windows script in a .plan file tied to a user account. The ClickFix command that invokes finger is, itself, obfuscated (in a rudimentary way) by breaking up the characters that make up the command with a comma, caret (^), hyphen, and underscore characters, which the Windows command interface helpfully ignores. The command, pasted into a text editor, looks like this:

Figure 4: The ClickFix command text

The command itself is not readily visible in the Run dialog because the threat actors have crafted the command line with a suffix that uses extra spaces and hyphen characters to trail the actual command. To an end user, the effect is that the content of the Run dialog seems to say, simply, "Push the Enter key."

Figure 5: The Run dialog conceals the command

The effect of the command line, however, is far from benign. It instructs the Windows command interface to execute the content contained within the .plan file at the other end of the command finger DLVBUCeFfF@grillrecipespro[.]com.

Figure 6: The top of the adversary-controlled user account's .plan file

The script content inside the remote .plan file is "hidden" with the use of 68 extra carriage-returns that put the weaponized content beyond the screen height of a typical terminal console. (Finger commands transmit plaintext over port 79/tcp by default, which should make them easy to detect or block, but since nobody uses finger anymore, most networks don't block this content.)

Well below the top of the screen, the .plan file contains a script with instructions to trigger the first stage of the attack, which requires an executable Python interpreter named ipyw32.exe that is included in a Python distribution called IronPython. So the script spawns curl to download and unpack IronPython.3.4.2.zip from its repository location, github[.]com/IronLanguages/ironpython3/releases/download/v3.4.2/IronPython.3.4.2.zip.

Figure 7: Don't you love it when a .plan comes together?

"The script places the IronPython ZIP file in the user's Temp directory, as a file with a .pdf extension." It then uses the tar command (which is now a part of modern Windows installations) to unpack the .zip; The script then navigates to the \net462 folder inside the nested structure of the unzipped archive, and passes a Base64-encoded, zlib-compressed Python script data blob directly to the ipyw32.exe program as a command flag.

The end result of this process retrieves and executes the content from hxxp://grillmasterchef[.]com/90e4a147-1234-505c-a024-062e543b5df8/timer6, and this is where it gets interesting.

Stage 2: Begin the barbeque

The timer6 file is a Python script that has been encoded in Base64, which has then had some of the latin alphabet characters substituted with cyrillic letters. Since the Base64 encoding scheme doesn't interpret cyrillic characters, a straight decode won't work. The script reverses the substitution of these alternate letters back to ASCII characters, then decodes the Base64 blob.

Figure 8: The top of the still-encoded timer6 Base64 (cyrillic lowercase letter "Yo" highlighted), with the script's cyrillic character/latin character substitution rules (inset)

Several cybersecurity vendors appear to believe that timer6 leverages a now-deprecated adversary simulation framework called Veil, which was designed to obfuscate Metasploit Meterpreter Python scripts to make them less easily detectable during penetration testing. That's arguably accurate, but not entirely correct: In reviewing the timer6 script, it appears to leverage some aspects of Veil's Python shellcode_inject/flat.py—in particular, it contains the same HeapCreate flag, HeapAlloc flag, buffer-copy pattern, and native API sequence. Veil explicitly describes this module as designed for inline shellcode injection, which is one thing that timer6 does. But there are other aspects of timer6's behavior that stray from what the full Veil package does by default.

The content of timer6, after decoding, is another Python script.

Figure 9: The second layer of timer6, a Python script decoded from Base64, which contains another decoding layer for XORed data that has been Base64 encoded

This shellcode layer is protected with a 19-byte XOR key (Hex: 84 0d ff da 80 29 b6 1b 52 9b 42 40 5d 55 aa 80 a5 7e 7c) that is embedded within the script as a separate Base64 blob.

Figure 10: The XOR key is in the house with you right now

When unpacked and decoded, the output of this script is a Windows PE malware loader, which executes as soon as the script decodes it. This malware loader searches the disk for a specific .ini file that contains a URL. If it finds the URL in the .ini file, it downloads whatever is at the other end (using the User-Agent string Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36), then performs RC4 decryption of the downloaded file.

In this instance, the loader connected to another barbeque-themed URL, hxxps://grillmasterchef[.]com/90e4a147-1234-505c-a024-062e543b5df8/v6, and decrypted the contents, which was another malware executable. The RC4 decryption key is prepended as the first 64 bytes of this v6 file.

The v6 malware, once decrypted, is automatically injected into memory by the script. The security vendor consensus is that this is a malware called Doina, which can serve as a delivery mechanism for other malware. In 2024, security vendor Halcyon reported that Doina was implicated as a precursor step to ransomware attacks, but Doina has multiple features and a modular architecture that make it useful as a general-purpose RAT, infostealer, and profiler tool.

Immediately after Doina began running, it began to communicate with the same grillmasterchef server from which it originated, sending a series of HTTPS POST communications, then retrieving a ZIP file from the URL hxxps://kiriosyka[.]com/KsxmmKiN5N0j/sqr-viewertr6: a 52MB compressed file that contains a full, portable instance of the Node.js code interpreter, and a malicious, heavily obfuscated index.js script. The malware unpacks this to the location C:\ProgramData\NodeView, then runs the (non-malicious) node.exe interpreter, passing it the index.js file as an argument.

Figure 11: Unzipped contents of the sqr-viewertr6 file

It's also notable that other elements of this attack deploy their various payloads, logs, and related files to both the root of the C:\ProgramData\ path, and to folders beneath that directory.

Stage 3: Cranking up the heat with more malware

While the index.js is a form of malware in its own right, it is also designed with a modular architecture that can download, decrypt, and inject various kinds of encrypted malicious payloads into memory as fileless malware.

In this investigation, the Node component pulled down two additional files, which then began beaconing and performing malware-esque activities. The two files were given randomized names that resemble GUIDs; One is only about 17KB in size, the other greater than 19MB in size. Neither has a discernible PE header, and both have high entropy. So what's going on here?

All three files are part of a package. The index.js component decrypts both files using AES-256-GCM, in which the first 12 bytes of each file is the nonce value, and the next 16 bytes are the key. It then executes the smaller file.

It turns out that the smaller of the two files is a shellcode reflective DLL injector (or sRDI), essentially a loader for the larger file. The larger file is an infostealer malware, allegedly Lumma Stealer. The sRDI component injects the stealer into memory through process hollowing, and the malware immediately begins beaconing.

As part of its initial check-in with its C2, the stealer malware transmits the hostname, username, and other profiling information as part of an initial HTTPS POST connection. It then switches gears and communicates over the websocket protocol for continuous monitoring.

Figure 12: Packet capture of websocket session traffic generated by the malware, receiving file name conventions to search for from the C2 server (red), and sending a unique identifier and "heartbeat" during idle time (blue).

The websocket connection included the URL pointing to the suspected Lumma Stealer download package, as well as filenames and other strings indicating software targets of interest to the stealer:

Browsers (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Opera)

Cryptocurrency wallet apps (Ledger, Electrum, Atomic Wallet)

Password managers (LastPass, Dashlane, 1Password, NordPass, RoboForm)

Email clients

Command processors like PowerShell

As with many of the other elements of this attacker infrastructure, the C2 addresses the malware communicates with are all themed around barbeque: thegrilljournal[.]com and homelygrill[.]com are used for exfil after an initial check-in to perfectgrillrecipes[.]com. The malware originates from the domain liokida[.]com (which, as far as we can tell, is not a barbeque term), and the stealer contains this domain embedded inside itself as a string. An earlier version of the attack also linked to the stealer payload from kiriosyka[.]com.

Interestingly, there are two forms of periodic updates that the Node malware, index.js performs: It can call for an update file that contains both the stealer and the reflective loader executable payloads and the Node.js interpreter files (which total at roughly 58MB in size), or it can retrieve just the payload files (index.js and the two .tmp files, at just under 20MB). To get the smaller-sized update, the malware calls the same URL with the query string ?exclude_bins=true at the end.

Every file retrieval request returns an archive with a unique hash, because the server hosting these payloads appends a random amount of null bytes to the archive at the time of the request. The payload inside the archive files changed once or twice per day.

Figure 13: Unzipped contents of the sqr-viewertr6 file downloaded with the exclude_bins=true query string, which does not include the Node executable

Finally, we observed yet another malicious component installed as part of the delivery of this malware package: A pirated copy of an RMM called NetSupport was also deployed inside the C:\ProgramData directory under the nonstandard folder Prodclear. The license key and copyright information for this RMM indicate the RMM is at least eight years old. The RMM maintains extensive log files of its activity within a subdirectory.

NetSupport's communication happens over an HTTPS connection that uses the nonstandard port 725/tcp, and this particular installation communicates with the IP address 167.148.201[.]106. The C2 traffic generated by the NetSupport Client software connects to the HTML file fakeurl.htm at the same IP address.

Figure 14: The NetSupport Client software executable was cryptographically signed eight years ago.

Stage 4: Chef Boyardon't and the Gastro Infra

As previously mentioned, the c2 and payload delivery .com domains used by the malware mostly sound like titles of a high-end magazine about cooking with charcoal: GrillRecipesPro, TheGrillJournal, EmbersAndBites, GrillMasterChef, and HomelyGrill all serve as both C2 and payload delivery domains. We found several relations between the domains, from common hosting and DNS servers to multiple payloads communicating with or being delivered from the domains.

Figure 15: Relationship map tying together C2 domains and payload delivery domain Liokida to multiple Lumma Stealer executables

Figure 16: URL, domain, and file relationships between Doina C2 domains and payload delivery domain Kiriosyka

The decidedly non-foody domains Liokida and Kiriosyka host the Lumma Stealer/Node.js payload packages, as well as several other malicious payloads that were not called during this attack.

Figure 17: Common URL patterns used to deliver payloads from Kiriosyka and Liokida domains

We also observed an IP address (167.148.201.106) used as a C2 for the NetConnect Client RMM payload. The IP address is used solely for hosting the legitimate website for a restaurant based in Detroit, but that domain has not been observed being abused. The C2 traffic connected directly to the IP address.

Figure 18: IP address linked to a restaurant domain being used for C2 communications

Figure 19: The deobfuscated Doina code calls the Lumma Stealer download and executes it

Mitigation

The best defense against ClickFix is user awareness of what it is and how it works. The attacks succeed because a large proportion of users simply don't recognize the risk of following an on-screen prompt. If you've made it this far, please tell your colleagues, family, and friends what to watch for. No legitimate CAPTCHA should ever ask anyone to paste an arbitrary line of text into an operating system command prompt. It just isn't how CAPTCHAs work.

Google's paid ad function can unwittingly host malicious links, in a technique commonly known as malvertising. Back in August, Huntress analysts reverse-engineered a MacSync Stealer sample collected from an incident that began with the user clicking on a sponsored Google result after searching for how to install Claude on a Mac.

Luckily for defenders, the way Google ad-clicks are redirected for billing the advertiser leaves some key signifiers for detection: aclk in the URL path and gclid in the resulting query strings.

Figure 20: The identifiers that Google uses to bill advertisers when users click on a sponsored result

These parameters indicate that a user reached a site through a Google-sponsored ad, even if later redirects obscure the original source. Investigators can use these markers in browser history, proxy logs, or URL telemetry to reconstruct the ad-to-malicious-site chain and connect related campaigns or domains. Reporting these identifiers to Google can kneecap attackers by cutting off their access to the ad ecosystem (at least, until they create a new account and start again).

Huntress customers and partners have an additional tool in their arsenal: A new feature called Attack Reduction is available now as part of Huntress Managed ESPM Early Access. ClickFix attacks typically prompt Windows users to open the Windows Run dialog box in order to enter a command; This feature enables admins to toggle access to the Run dialog for the majority of users who never need it. (See how it works and what it blocks.)

Figure 21: Closeup of the Attack Reduction feature that prevents users from opening the Run dialog in ESPM Early Access

It doesn't stop every form of ClickFix—notably, attackers sometimes ask users to open PowerShell, the command prompt, or even to enter commands into the address bar in Windows Explorer—but it's a very commonly abused method that most people on managed endpoints won't miss.

As reported in our newly released Tragic Quadrant, ClickFix accounted for about 2.2% of the Managed Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) detection signals Huntress has seen this year so far, but nearly 99% of those detections were high severity. Posts on social media sites still show that lots of users are getting tricked into falling for a ClickFix scam on a daily basis.

Just one malicious command pasted into a Run box can open the door to infostealers, remote access tools, ransomware, or other malicious software. The results can be devastating, leading to financial loss and, potentially, compromise of an entire enterprise. But just like we learned to look both ways before crossing the street, we'll learn not to do anything a dialog box on a web page tells us to do, just because it asks. An ounce of skepticism is worth hours of remediation.

Title: Attack Reduction in Huntress Managed ESPM: Disrupting ClickFix
Context: Introducing Attack Reduction Attack Reduction is a new capability in Huntress Managed ESPM that turns off Windows features your users never touch, but attackers rely on,...
Full Text:
Mandy was stuck at an airport with a few hours to kill. She decided to get her nails done, so she found a spa listed on the airport's website and clicked through. It looked like the spa's real website, on a normal domain with HTTPS, and Chrome showed no warnings.

Then a CAPTCHA popped up. Nothing too unusual there. It asked for a few "verification steps" to ensure she was a human user:

Press and hold Windows key + R

In the verification window, press Ctrl + V

Press Enter

An example ClickFix attack where a user is told to press "Windows Key + R" and paste a command into the Run dialog that opens.

But this simple sequence of hotkeys actually opens the Windows Run dialog, and in this case, would have pasted a malicious PowerShell command that the webpage quietly copied to the clipboard. (The Windows Run dialog is a small box that lets you type a command or program name and run it right away.)

If Mandy pressed Enter, the command would have downloaded and run a file from the internet. That file sets up persistence through a registry key, installs a remote access trojan, and steals the browser's saved passwords, cookies, and credit card details.

This is not a hypothetical example. This actually happened to a Huntress employee (name changed for privacy). Thankfully, she realized what was going on and didn't get pwned. A LOT of people aren't so lucky. So, this post is about one simple idea: what if "Windows key + R" didn't open anything at all?

What is ClickFix, and why is it everywhere?

ClickFix is a simple social engineering attack that tricks users into running malicious commands they don't understand. It often employs messaging related to fixing a problem, hence the name "ClickFix."

It also works very well. Our 2026 Cyber Threat Report linked ClickFix and fake CAPTCHA scams to over half of all malware loader activity. In our own SOC, ClickFix-style Run dialog attacks now account for 31% of EDR SOC signals.

The lures keep changing: fake Windows Update screens, fake Docker ads, compromised small-business websites, and now malicious AI chatbots. But the classic version almost always ends the same way, with Windows key + R.

Most of your users should never open the Run dialog

Here's what makes this so frustrating. The Run dialog is a power-user shortcut. IT folks love it. Most employees have never opened it on purpose and wouldn't know what to type into it if they did.

We've seen this play out in the data. Across organizations in ESPM Early Access, it's common to see 90% or more of users who never use the Run dialog at all. Which is why they don't recognize the commands they are pasting in as being a problem.

Run dialog box on Windows in which a user has pasted a malicious command, unwittingly copied from a ClickFix attack.

That's a big gap. A feature almost nobody needs is the starting point for nearly a third of what our EDR SOC investigates. Detection still matters, and Huntress Managed EDR's Attack Disruption engine can kill many ClickFix chains in under a second. But when the attack depends on a feature your users don't need, the simplest fix is to turn that feature off. If only there was an easy way to do that…Oh, wait, now there is!

Introducing Attack Reduction

Attack Reduction is a new capability in Huntress Managed ESPM that turns off Windows features your users never touch, but attackers rely on, starting with "Windows key + R". That fits what ESPM is built to do: harden your endpoints before an attack ever starts.

ESPM Attack Reduction dashboard

We're starting with the Run dialog, because that's where ClickFix starts. More controls are coming:

Available now: Blocking the Run dialog for users who don't need it to disrupt "Windows key + R" attacks.

Planned: Command Prompt restrictions for users who don't use cmd.exe.

Planned: Interactive PowerShell restrictions for users who don't use it.

Planned: Windows Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rules that stop Office, script, and email apps from launching or injecting payloads.

Planned: Blocking HTML applications (mshta) for users who don't use them.

How Attack Reduction works

The hard part of turning off a Windows feature isn't flipping the switch. It's knowing who will be affected and not breaking legitimate workflows. Attack Reduction is designed with the following in mind.

1. See who actually uses the Run dialog

Once ESPM is on, Attack Reduction collects each user's Run dialog history and builds a baseline. On the Attack Reduction dashboard, you can see which users rely on the Run dialog and which never touch it, across your whole account or one organization at a time. You'll know exactly who would be affected before anything changes.

The dashboard also flags commands in a user's Run history that look like ClickFix. Windows doesn't record when those commands ran, so treat them as a reason to investigate rather than proof of an active attack.

The ESPM Attack Reduction dashboard and how many users are utilizing the Run dialog per week.

2. Turn on blocking

When you're ready, turn on blocking at the account or organization level. Attack Reduction then turns off the "Windows key + R" shortcut for users who don't need it. Users who rely on the Run dialog can keep it, and you can switch any user between allowed and blocked at any time.

3. Users get a clear message, not a mystery

If a blocked user presses Windows key + R, nothing runs. Instead, they see a pop-up explaining that the action was blocked for security reasons and asking them to contact their IT support team or take Security Awareness Training. Either way, the attack stops, and a confused user gets a quick security lesson.

4. You get a record of what they almost ran

When a blocked user presses Windows key + R, Attack Reduction also captures what was on their clipboard. If someone was about to paste a malicious command, you'll have it on record, which helps you spot users who are being targeted and follow up.

The ESPM Attack Reduction dashboard and a list of blocked attempts by users to utilize the Run dialog.

What Attack Reduction doesn't do

We want to be clear about the limits here, because ClickFix is a moving target.

Blocking the Run dialog disrupts the most common version of ClickFix. It doesn't stop every one. Attackers can, and already do, tell users to paste commands into File Explorer's address bar, Windows Terminal, Command Prompt, or PowerShell instead.

That's why the Run dialog is the first step, not the last one. Every path we close makes the attack harder to pull off, and the planned Command Prompt and PowerShell controls are aimed at exactly those next moves. Attack Reduction also works best alongside the rest of your defenses: Managed EDR to catch what gets through, and Managed SAT so users know a real CAPTCHA will never ask them to paste a command.

Get started with Attack Reduction

Attack Reduction is available now as part of Huntress Managed ESPM Early Access for existing Huntress partners and customers.

Not in ESPM Early Access yet? Click the ESPM icon in the left-hand menu of your Huntress portal to enroll. Then let Attack Reduction collect a baseline so you can see which users actually need the Run dialog before flipping on Blocking.

As Early Access partners put this capability to work, their feedback will decide which Windows features we tackle next and how we build those controls.

Have ideas or requests? Share them at feedback.huntress.com/espm. And stay tuned. There's a lot more coming to Managed ESPM.

Full Text:
Acknowledgments: Special thanks to Lindsey Welch and Ben Nahorney for their contributions to this investigation and writeup.

Update 10/21/26 @ 4:40pm ET

Since PHP released its security advisory this morning to address the two critical vulnerabilities, several researchers have come forward to release the technical details of the vulnerabilities:

Calif's write-up provides a detailed history of PHP memory-limit vulnerabilities, and then explains how Calif revisited those earlier findings through OpenAI's Patch the Planet initiative, uncovering multiple interruption point and reliable RCE paths.

Wiz has demonstrated how the unauthenticated RCE works against WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla, and showed that a separate memory disclosure path could expose passwords, tokens, API keys, and certificates.

As of October 21 at 4:30pm ET, Huntress has not observed in-the-wild exploitation on partner systems. We are continuing to monitor relevant developments linked to these vulnerabilities.

Update: 10/21/26 @ 10am ET

On October 21 around 9:30 am ET, the PHP team released PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 to address the two vulnerabilities.

According to PHP, all PHP installations serving web requests are at risk (including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed). An exploit exists for mod_php where an unauthenticated request can trigger an attack before any application code runs.

What to do:

Source downloads are on PHP's downloads site; organizations should update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35 as soon as possible. For organizations that can't update immediately, PHP has also outlined measures to reduce exposure to specific attack paths in its advisory.

Other update guidance from PHP:

Linux distributions and LTS vendors received the patches ahead of publication. Check with your vendor for updated PHP packages.

PHP 8.1 and earlier are no longer supported by the PHP project and won't receive official updates. Some distributions and LTS vendors might backport fixes for these releases, so be sure to contact your vendor for further information or upgrade to a supported version.

Organizations using the volunteer-maintained rpms.remirepo.net repository should move to distribution-provided packages or build PHP from source to apply updates promptly. Updated packages from that repository won't be available today.

The PHP security team has also provided minimal source-backports for PHP 7.4, PHP 8.0, and PHP 8.1. These branches are intended for organizations that build PHP from source or don't have access to an LTS vendor.

For those running the older, outdated versions of PHP (prior to the 8.2.x version numbers), it's likely there will be no official patch to resolve the vulnerabilities. For environments running the deprecated, end-of-life versions of PHP, admins should immediately add the line session.upload_progress.enabled = Off to the php.ini configuration on your server. This may require you to restart your web services and/or the server itself in order to take effect, but will mitigate the known abuse cases.

While the software itself in these deprecated versions will receive no official patch from the PHP maintainers, security researchers have produced their own patches that will permit admins to rebuild the PHP modules from source code. Huntress cannot evaluate whether these patches are effective, and recommend that, wherever possible (and with adequate testing to ensure the upgrade doesn't break website functionality), admins should upgrade their version of PHP on the servers they maintain to the most current 8.5.x release.

The vulnerabilities:

PHP released further information about the two vulnerabilities.

CVE-2026-109618 is a remote code execution flaw in PHP's out-of-memory error handling. If PHP runs out of memory while setting up request data, it is interrupted and that data is only partially initialized. During request cleanup that partly initialized data is treated as valid, creating a path to code execution.

The impact here is unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) as the web worker account: according to PHP, complete RCE was validated over HTTP against mod_php with default PHP input and memory limits, and normal prefork configurations with multiple workers.

CVE-2026-109619 is a remote code execution flaw caused by PHP retaining request-specific state after its backing memory has been freed. If the same worker processes a later request, PHP may access that stale state before the normal initialization resets it. This vulnerability can lead to unauthenticated heap use-after-free, memory disclosure, and remote code execution with the web worker's privileges.

Huntress has not yet seen in-the-wild exploitation of these vulnerabilities across our partner base as of October 21 at 10am ET; however, others are reporting that they are seeing attacks emerging. As such, updating promptly to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35 and following the guidance above is critical.

Huntress is continuing to track developments related to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. We will update this blog accordingly as new information emerges.

Background

On the morning of October 20, a post on Hacker News claimed that two critical PHP vulnerabilities were headed for public disclosure. The post was taken down, but not before screenshots made their way around social media. Within a few hours, our good friends over at watchTowr confirmed the leak, writing that the vulnerabilities were real and that "we were all supposed to wait until Thursday at 11am ET."

Shortly thereafter, the PHP security team posted an advance notice of an upcoming security release addressing two critical vulnerabilities, both with a CVSS v4.0 rating of 9.2. The team scheduled that release for Wednesday, October 21 at 14:00 UTC, a day earlier than the original embargo, and noted it reserves the right to release even sooner "should details of either vulnerability become public, or should evidence of active exploitation appear in the wild."

PHP is everywhere. It quietly powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and an awful lot of software that doesn't even advertise that it runs PHP under the hood. When a critical bug lands in PHP itself, rather than in one app built on top of it, the number of places you have to go looking to identify vulnerable PHP versions gets very big, very fast.

Huntress is monitoring developments related to these vulnerabilities and will update this blog as new information becomes available.

What are CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619?

The flaws exist in PHP, the popular programming language running behind a huge number of websites. PHP is designed primarily for web development and is widely supported by hosting providers.

Here's what we know about the PHP vulnerabilities so far (and what we don't):

What we know: Both vulnerabilities are rated critical by the PHP security team. Public reporting describes them as remote code execution in PHP's core, which would mean an attacker could get the server to run commands of their choosing.

What it affects: PHP has not published affected versions yet. Reports have pointed to versions 5, 6, 7, and 8 being impacted, and some researchers have said they expect fixes only for currently supported PHP 8 branches. In its official release, however, PHP said that impacted and fixed versions (along with full details of the flaws) will be published with the October 21 security release.

How it works: No technical root cause has been published. We currently don't yet know which part of PHP is involved, whether it's reachable over a plain web request, or whether it depends on a particular configuration. We'll update this post when the advisory and researcher writeups are public.

Why "php2shell"? That's the name circulating among researchers. If you've followed this space for any amount of time, you know a name like that usually means one thing: someone sends a request to your website, and gets a shell on your vulnerable server.

Technical Details

With no public technical details yet, we can't show you the exploit. What we can do is tell you what we're looking for and what our own telemetry says about where the risk lives.

What exploitation will probably look like

Florian Roth, who released a free tool called process-watcher (a Linux-based process monitoring tool aimed at detecting exploitation) put it well: exploitation of these bugs will most likely show up as suspicious child processes spawned by PHP. At Huntress, that lines up with what we see in nearly every PHP intrusion we work.

In practice, that means a PHP worker process like php-fpm, php-cgi, php-cgi.exe, httpd, or apache2 would launch something abnormal:

Shells like sh, bash, cmd.exe, or powershell.exe

Interpreters like python or perl

Download or networking tools like curl, wget, nc, or certutil.exe

It's worth taking a closer look at command lines that include reverse shell patterns:

/dev/tcp/

fsockopen

mkfifo

It's also worth looking at quick reconnaissance commands like whoami, id, uname -a, or ipconfig run straight from the web server.

Attacker PHP abuse: what we've seen recently

Even before this leak, Huntress regularly catches attackers abusing PHP applications.

One pattern from a recent Huntress incident that occurred last week is a good preview of what php2shell exploitation could look like. In this incident, a PHP FastCGI process repeatedly ran a one-liner that wrote a small PHP file with random marker strings into the first writable temp directory it could find, before executing and then deleting it. If none of the directories were writable, it would print !notwrtbl! to flag that.

While this pattern isn't related to php2shell, it's a good example of PHP spawning things it shouldn't.

On the Linux side, most internet-facing PHP lives on web servers and shared hosting, which are not closely monitored. An exposed Linux web server without endpoint detection is the type of system where PHP flaws can be exploited quietly and remain unnoticed.

Proof of Concept

We have not built or reproduced a proof of concept for these vulnerabilities, and we're not aware of public exploit code as of this writing. A short exploitation video was briefly posted online and then removed. Once fixes are shipped, we expect technical details and proof-of-concept code to follow quickly, and we'll update this post.

What should impacted organizations do?

The fixes aren't out yet, so the goal right now is to be ready to patch the minute they land. In the meantime, there are several things you can do to shrink your exposure.

Inventory every PHP install. Start with your web servers, and then go hunting for the less obvious locations: vendor appliances and Windows software that bundle php.exe or php-cgi.exe, control panels like cPanel and Plesk, and anything running WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, or Magento.

Plan your patch window for Wednesday, October 21 at 10am ET. Patch internet-facing systems first. Watch the official PHP announcement for the fixed version numbers, and check your Linux distribution and hosting provider for backported packages.

Identify any end-of-life PHP environments. If you're running PHP 5, 7, or 8.0/8.1, you may not get a fix at all. Upgrade, take it off the internet, or put it behind a VPN or web application firewall (WAF) until you can.

Keep an eye on what PHP spawns. Alert on PHP worker processes launching shells, interpreters, or download tools. On Linux servers without endpoint detection, Florian Roth's process-watcher is a free, quick way to get this visibility today. Start it in observe mode.

If you find something, isolate the server, and preserve web server and PHP logs. Look for webshells and new files in your web root, along with new cron jobs, scheduled tasks, and accounts.

What is Huntress doing?

Hunting across our fleet. We captured a baseline of normal PHP behavior across our partner endpoints before the release. Once fixes and technical details drop, we'll compare against it to spot new activity quickly.

We already monitor for malicious activity on servers. Huntress already detects web server processes spawning shells and common webshell activity on Windows and Linux. Our SOC is on alert for PHP-related activity.

Watching the patch drop. Our Adversary Tactics team is tracking the release and researcher analysis in real time, and we'll update this post with indicators and detection guidance as they become available.

Auditing our internal PHP use. Huntress has reviewed relevant internal systems and taken appropriate steps to mitigate potential exposure to these vulnerabilities.

Sigma / YARA Rules

We'll publish detection rules to huntresslabs/threat-intel once technical details are available.

Indicators of Compromise (IOCs)

No indicators of compromise have been confirmed yet. This section will be updated as the situation develops.

Today, Huntress Managed ITDR's Lookback feature is generally available for newly onboarded Microsoft 365 tenants. Lookback automatically examines up to 180 days of login history to uncover evidence of compromise before Huntress connected. When a compromise is still active, our Security Operations Center (SOC) investigates and revokes the identity's active sessions.

Onboarding a Microsoft 365 tenant feels like a fresh start. You go through your checklist, and a successful connection tells you monitoring has started. But it doesn't tell you if an attacker got there first. Your first day protecting a tenant might be an attacker's twenty-seventh day inside.

That's what Lookback seeks to solve. You get a clearer picture of the tenant you've inherited, plus defenders who act on what they find. And yes, that includes trial tenants.

Six months of login history. A much stronger start.

Lookback runs once, automatically, when a Microsoft 365 tenant finishes onboarding to Managed ITDR. There's nothing extra to configure and no separate scan to remember to launch.

Huntress Managed ITDR's new Lookback feature is generally available, bringing up to 180 days of Microsoft 365 login history into the hunt for existing compromises.

Lookback applies Huntress's full set of Unwanted Access detections to the tenant's available Microsoft 365 login history, looking back up to 180 days. That includes detections for credential theft, token theft, adversary-in-the-middle attacks, suspicious browsers, and datacenter logins.

Here's the tricky part: evidence of an old compromise doesn't necessarily mean an attacker still has access. Someone may have already reset the password or revoked the compromised sessions. Treating every historical finding as a fresh emergency would make onboarding pretty miserable.

Lookback separates findings based on whether the compromise is still active:

Active compromises receive a critical Incident Report investigated by the Huntress AI-centric SOC, with the identity's active sessions revoked. This turns historical evidence into a reason to act right away.

Previously remediated compromises appear in the Identity Security Assessment as historical context. They don't trigger a new incident or an unnecessary lockdown for something you've already fixed.

Lookback is part of onboarding for newly connected Microsoft 365 tenants.
